title: An Analysis of the Focused Jump-and-Repair EA on Parameterized Max-2-Sat
abstract: Evolutionary algorithms are often used in practice to tackle NP-hard optimization problems. However, comparatively few theoretical analyses exist for these types of problems since they are significantly more complex than simple benchmarks. Moreover, it is not always clear how best to design algorithm components for these domains. Recently, ideas from the field of parameterized algorithmics have been applied to the theoretical analysis of simple randomized search heuristics on NP-hard problems. By using a finer-grained analysis informed by problem parameters, these approaches can yield a sharper understanding of the influence of problem structure on algorithm behavior, and aid in the development of operators with provably good performance.We consider the NP-hard Max-2-Sat problem parameterized by the number of false clauses in an optimal solution. We design a probabilistic repair operator for 2SAT formulas as module for the (1+1) EA with focused jump and repair introduced by Branson and Sutton [FOGA, 2021]. We prove that the resulting algorithm solves Max-2-Sat in expected time \(O(12^km\log n)\) where m is the formula size, n is the number of variables and k is the count of clauses that are false in an optimal solution. This establishes that the algorithm is an FPT randomized search heuristic for parameterized Max-2-Sat. We complement our theoretical results with computational experiments.

title: Runtime Analysis of a Compact Genetic Algorithm on a Truly Multi-Valued OneMax Function
abstract: Recently, the runtime analysis of multi-valued estimation-of-distribution algorithms in the framework of Ben Jedidia et al. (TCS 2024) has made significant advancements. However, almost all existing analyses are limited to multi-valued objective functions that in each dimension only distinguish between two types, also called categories, of values and hence can be treated with similar methods as pseudo-Boolean problems. Only recently, Adak and Witt (GECCO 2025) have presented a first runtime analysis of a multi-valued compact genetic algorithm (cGA) on the multi-valued OneMax function G–OneMax\(:\) \(\{0,\dots ,r-1\}^n \rightarrow \mathbb {N}\) defined by G–OneMax\((\boldsymbol{x}_1,\dots ,\boldsymbol{x}_n)=\sum _{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i\) and truly depending on all r categories. We improve their runtime result from \(\textrm{O}(n r^3 \log ^2( n)\log (r))\) to \(\textrm{O}(n r \log ^3(n)\log ^3(r))\), both for an optimal choice of the update strength K. Our result matches, up to polylogarithmic factors, the existing bound for the simpler r-valued OneMax function depending essentially only on two values and analyzed in several previous works. To show the new bound, we use improved drift theorems for processes with high self-loop probabilities and specifically derived concentration inequalities to analyze how probability mass in the multi-valued cGA moves into successively smaller and smaller intervals of the r-valued frequency matrix.

title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming in Evolving Boolean Functions
abstract: Cartesian Genetic Programming (CGP) is among the practical and popular forms of Genetic Programming as it uses a graph-based representation of programs. This paper presents a first runtime analysis of CGP in evolving Boolean functions using complete training sets. We prove an asymptotic bound \(O(nD^5)\) for the expected number of fitness evaluations of CGP to construct a conjunction of n inputs using at most \(D\ge n-1\) binary gates, a minimal function set, and even with a strict survival selection. When the non-strict selection is used, the bound is improved to \(O(nD^4)\). Our analysis reveals interesting characteristics of CGP induced search, which have been only observed empirically. In particular, enabling the acceptance of equally good solutions, including those with connected gates non-contributing to fitness, can lead to a speedup, and consequently a better asymptotic time bound. In contrast to conjunctions, we also prove a negative result which shows that CGP requires exponential time to evolve an exclusive disjunction. Experiments evolving conjunctions complement our theoretical findings. The use of incomplete training sets is found to further reduce the average number of fitness evaluations while maintaining a good level of generalisation.

title: Runtime Analysis of the (1+1) EA on Plateau Functions of Multi-valued Decision Variables
abstract: There has been a recent interest in the theory community to investigate the runtime of various randomized search heuristics optimizing functions of multi-valued decision variables. In this setting, it is not always clear how algorithm behavior changes when moving to higher cardinality alphabets. Moreover, the algebraic ring structure within each variable suggests new kinds of search operators. In this paper, we study the (1+1) EA optimizing functions over \(\{0,1,\ldots ,q-1\}^n\) for any \(q > 1\) in which large plateaus must be traversed. Recently, Doerr and Kelley [Algorithmica, 2024] connected discrete Fourier analysis to the plateau behavior of the (1+1) EA on functions over \(\{0,1\}^n\). We extend this work to q-ary strings for arbitrary q by expressing the mutation distribution in the orthogonal basis of complex Fourier functions which are characters of the abelian group . We prove exact and tight asymptotic bounds for the (1+1) EA using standard uniform mutation on the multi-valued Needle and RoyalRoad functions. We adapt the analysis to prove coarser upper and lower bounds on the (1+1) EA using a less aggressive cycle mutation operator that recognizes the ring structure of each variable. We also conduct experiments to observe how the accuracy of the bounds on cycle mutation depend on q.

title: The $$(1+1)\text {-EA} $$ in Dynamic Environments
abstract: We study the \((1+1)\text {-EA} \) in dynamic linear environments, where in every generation selection is based on a freshly sampled linear function with positive weights. We consider the Dynamic Binary Value problem, where each generation uses a uniformly random permutation of \(1,2,4,\dots ,2^{n-1}\), and a Uniform weight variant, where the weights are drawn independently from \(\textrm{Unif}(0,1)\). Both of them have recently been integrated into the IOHprofiler platform and empirically studied.For both models we prove a sharp threshold in the mutation parameter \(\chi \) for mutation rate \(\chi /n\). Below the threshold, the expected optimisation time is \(\mathcal {O}{(n\log n)}\), whereas above it the runtime becomes \(2^{\varOmega {(n)}}\).For the Dynamic Binary Value problem in the exponential regime, we also quantify at what distance from the optimum the optimisation process stagnates. We show that there is a second threshold: a distance that is efficiently reached, but reaching any smaller distance takes exponential time. This quantifies and proves previous empirical findings.

title: Theoretical Analysis of the (1+1)-EA-ES with Reduced Success Rule for Mixed Discrete–Continuous Optimization
abstract: We introduce and analyze the (1+1)-EA-ES for mixed discrete–continuous optimization, combining a bitflip operator for discrete coordinates with a Gaussian mutation and a step size adapted via success rules for continuous coordinates. We show that the discrete component of the search—especially when close to optimal—can hinder progress in the continuous part by reducing the overall success probability. This disrupts the step size adaptation mechanism of the continuous component and may lead to premature convergence.We formally prove that on SphereOneMax, for large enough dimensions, a reduced target success probability can bypass this problem. More precisely, we prove for the (1+1)-EA-ES with reduced success probability a bound on the expected time to reach an epsilon neighborhood of the optimum in \(\mathcal {O}\left( \max \left\{ n_c,n_d \right\} \cdot \left( \log (1/\varepsilon ) + n_d + 1/n_c \right) \right) \) where \(n_c\) represents the number of continuous variables and \(n_d\) the number of discrete ones.

title: A Bi-heuristic Initialized NSGA-II Algorithm for Multi-skilled Human-Robot Collaborative Disassembly Line Balancing Considering Robot Technology Tiers and Operator Experience Levels
abstract: The rapid expansion of electric vehicles and renewable energy storage systems has made the efficient recovery of end-of-life batteries a critical global challenge. To support a sustainable circular economy, optimizing human-robot collaborative (HRC) disassembly lines is essential for maximizing resource recovery while controlling operational costs. However, the disassembly line balancing problem (DLBP) is inherently NP-hard, making the optimal assignment of tasks and resources an intractable computational task. In modern hybrid manufacturing environments, integrating multi-skilled (MS) resources with varying robot technology tiers (RTT) and operator experience levels (OEL) is vital, as these factors directly dictate execution speed, flexibility, and total costs. This study proposes a novel bi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model for the MS-HRCDLBP to simultaneously minimize cycle time and total disassembly cost. To solve this problem, the augmented epsilon-constraint (AUGMECON2) algorithm is used to validate the quality of solutions of smaller instances, while a customized hybrid non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (HNSGA-II) with a bi-heuristic initialization strategy is developed for large-scale instances. The proposed approach is validated using an industrial case study on EV battery disassembly, along with adapted benchmark datasets comprising up to 89 tasks. The computational results demonstrate that HNSGA-II effectively overcomes the computational limitations of the exact solver, successfully identifying high-quality Pareto-optimal trade-offs and providing decision-makers with diverse and cost-effective resource allocation strategies.

title: Accelerating Lagrangian Relaxation via Dual-Guided Genetic Search for UAV Trajectory and Camera Orientation Optimization
abstract: This paper addresses unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path optimization with integrated viewpoint selection and camera orientation planning. The proposed framework captures the intricate interdependencies among these decisions and optimizes them simultaneously for the first time, balancing surface coverage quality and flight energy consumption. To tackle this large-scale combinatorial problem, a Lagrangian relaxation approach decomposes the model into an orienteering subproblem and a coverage subproblem. A Genetic Algorithm (GA) with a dual-guided mutation operator efficiently solves the orienteering subproblem. Theoretical analysis and empirical validation are provided. Experimental results demonstrate that the dual-guided genetic search reduces runtime by 51.3% and improves the weighted objective by 9.3% over a standard genetic algorithm. Moreover, it matches or improves upon an exact mixed-integer linear programming solver while cutting runtime by over 90% on small instances and by 50–70% on larger ones.

title: Determining Destroy Sets in Large Neighborhood Search by Generative Flow Networks
abstract: Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) is an often applied metaheuristic for solving challenging combinatorial optimization problems. Typically, it relies on the scheme of iteratively removing parts of a solution by one or more destroy operators and cleverly augmenting the solution again by repair operators. Destroy operators are usually handcrafted and often a mixture of uniform random selection and problem-specific heuristics, and their choice can dramatically impact the performance. Inspired by the recent success of Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), we propose their usage to compile promising destroy sets. These generative deep learning models stand out in that their goal is not to learn a single high-reward structure but to produce diverse structures according to a complex probability density function. As considering many different but promising destroy sets is fundamental in LNS, we believe GFlowNets to be well suited for this purpose. We study an intentionally generic and simple LNS framework and apply it to three hard graph problems. The only problem-specific part is the repair operator that is realized by basic iterated random construction heuristics. When applying the best GFlowNet model, the effectiveness of the LNS is on average increased by 6.52% in terms of online performance compared to a corresponding baseline LNS. Moreover, a comparison to integer linear programming models solved by Gurobi shows that they are clearly dominated by our GFlowNet-guided LNS on the considered hard benchmark instances with a mean relative improvement of 20.73% in terms of final solution quality.

title: Effective Traveling for Metric Instances of the Traveling Thief Problem
abstract: The Traveling Thief Problem (TTP) is a multi-component optimization problem that captures the interplay between routing and packing decisions by combining the classical Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and the Knapsack Problem (KP). The TTP has gained significant attention in the evolutionary computation literature and a wide range of approaches have been developed over the last 10 years. Judging the performance of these algorithms in particular in terms of how close the get to optimal solutions is a very challenging task as effective exact methods are not available due to the highly challenging traveling component. In this paper, we study the tour-optimization component of TTP under a fixed packing plan. We formulate this task as a weighted variant of the TSP, where travel costs depend on the cumulative weight of collected items, and investigate how different distance metrics and cost functions affect computational complexity. We present an \(O(n^2)\)-time dynamic programming algorithm for the path metric with general cost functions, prove that the problem is NP-hard even on a star metric, and develop constant-factor approximation algorithms for star metrics. We complement our theoretical results with experimental evaluations on standard TTP instances adjusted to a path metric. Our experimental results demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our approaches by comparing it to solutions produced by popular iterative search algorithms. The results show that our methods are able to significantly improve the quality of solutions for some benchmark instances by optimizing the traveling part while pointing out the optimality of the travel component for other solutions obtained by iterative search methods.

title: Efficient AB-Cycle Fusion: Boosting GPX and Assessing Its Impact on EAX
abstract: Many highly effective solvers have been developed for the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), among which the Edge Assembly Crossover (EAX) and the Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun (LKH) heuristic are considered state of the art. In recent years, Generalized Partition Crossover (GPX) has emerged as a promising crossover operator that preserves all parental edges. It might thus be beneficial in situations in which EAX loses important information during the search. However, existing GPX variants lack a competitive implementation and are unable to reliably determine the feasibility of fused AB-cycles. In this work, we extend a recently proposed subtour-check procedure for AB-cycles to improve the evaluation of fused AB-cycles within GPX. Based on this extension, we develop a new GPX variant and integrate it directly into EAX. Unlike previous GPX variants, which rely on restrictive feasibility criteria such as equal connections or mirror-edge tests, our approach can correctly determine the feasibility of arbitrary fused AB-cycles. This overcomes a major limitation of previous GPX implementations. We evaluate the resulting algorithm on a well-established benchmark of evolved TSP instances and show that it outperforms vanilla EAX in several settings. To better understand the impact and limitations of our proposed check, we analyze the interaction between the two stages of EAX and the distribution of optimal edges in the population. Our experiments indicate that EAX sometimes removes optimal edges from the population during the first stage, thereby limiting the potential benefit of GPX in later stages. These findings provide new insight into the behavior of EAX and suggest promising directions for future research on crossover operators and population initialization.

title: Beyond IGO-Flow: Toward Convergence Analysis of IGO in Continuous Spaces
abstract: Information-Geometric Optimization (IGO) provides a unified framework for black-box optimization by interpreting the adaptation of a search distribution as a natural gradient update. Despite its conceptual importance, the convergence theory of IGO remains limited: most existing results concern continuous-time idealizations such as the IGO flow, rather than discrete-time updates with non-infinitesimal learning rates. In this paper, we study discrete-time IGO in continuous spaces, formulated as natural gradient updates in the expectation-parameter coordinates of an exponential family. In particular, we analyze IGO over the multivariate Gaussian family on strongly convex quadratic objective functions. Our analysis covers a setting that simultaneously incorporates full covariance adaptation, a fixed positive learning rate, and quantile-based weights. In this setting, we prove that the covariance matrix converges to the zero matrix. We further show that the mean vector converges to the global optimum, provided that the condition number of the appropriately scaled covariance matrix is bounded at sufficiently frequent iterations. These results advance the convergence theory of IGO and help bridge the gap between the mathematical theory of IGO and practical covariance-adaptive search methods such as CMA-ES.

title: Evolutionary Latent Space Search for Real-Time Dynamic Vehicle Routing Under Demand and Traffic Uncertainty
abstract: Dynamic Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems (DVRPs) require real-time routing decisions under continuously changing demand and traffic conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches generate a single solution per inference step, limiting flexibility in dynamic environments. We propose a Latent Vector-Guided Evolutionary Inference Method (LVGEIM) that maintains a population of latent vector individuals in the continuous policy space to guide parallel route decoding during inference. At each step, the population is updated via elitism, Gaussian perturbation, and random immigration, enabling gradient-free adaptation to shifting conditions without modifying the policy network. A lightweight two-stream encoding architecture separates static and dynamic features to enable efficient parallel inference. Evaluations across four problem scales and six uncertainty scenarios show that LVGEIM consistently outperforms competitive baselines including POMO, achieving lower routing cost across all tested conditions while remaining real-time.

title: From Small to Large: A Heuristic Divide-and-Neural-Conquer Framework for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing Problems
abstract: Although Neural Combinatorial Optimization models have shown promise in solving Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs), they suffer from severe performance degradation when scaling to large-scale instances beyond their training distribution. To overcome this scalability challenge, we propose Heuristic Divide-and-Neural-Conquer (HDNC), a novel framework that elegantly solves large-scale VRPs by conquering small-scale constituent sub-problems. Instead of relying on complex learning-based partitioning policies, HDNC utilizes lightweight heuristic strategies to efficiently decompose large-scale instances into manageable sub-problems. Specifically, we introduce a grid/clustering method for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and a novel Adaptive Polar-Radial Decomposition for the Capacitated VRP (CVRP). These sub-problems are solved in parallel by a pre-trained neural solver, seamlessly integrated via a heuristic merging strategy, and further optimized through a refinement mechanism to ensure global consistency. Extensive experiments on TSP and CVRP demonstrate that HDNC achieves state-of-the-art performance. It exhibits superior robustness across diverse data distributions and significantly outperforms strong baselines on the challenging TSPLIB and CVRPLIB benchmarks.

title: HCPS: Heuristic Candidate-Space Policy Search for Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
abstract: Many real-world combinatorial optimization tasks are constrained constructive processes with expensive per-step fitness evaluation. Population-based methods often suffer from high evaluation cost, while single-solution methods may lack exploration. We propose Heuristic Candidate-space Policy Search (HCPS), a hybrid framework that combines heuristic candidate-space shaping with policy-based sequential selection. At each decision step, HCPS applies feasibility-aware Top-K pruning to compress the primitive action space and then uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to optimize long-horizon utility on the reduced candidate set. We provide complexity analysis showing that Top-K pruning can substantially reduce computation while keeping quality loss limited when high-value actions are retained with high probability. Experiments on agile Earth observation satellite scheduling as a representative testbed demonstrate a strong quality–time trade-off and support the framework’s generalizability.

title: Insights from Multi-tasking the EAX Algorithm for the Travelling Salesperson Problem
abstract: Evolutionary multitasking allows several related problems to be solved in a single run of an algorithm. In this paper, we investigate integrating evolutionary multitasking with Edge Assembly Crossover (MT-EAX) to solve the classical Travelling Salesperson Problem (TSP). To fairly compare MT-EAX against standard EAX under strict compute budgets, we evaluate three scaling methods: generation scaling, population scaling, and balanced scaling. Our results show that generationally scaled MT-EAX is highly effective compute-wise in the early stages of the search, saving \(60\%\) to \(90\%\) of compute for equal or better solution quality. We observe that instance geometry has a significant impact, with clustered, normally distributed instances securing larger improvements than uniformly distributed ones. However, when scaling by population or utilising explicit solution transfer, the results are negative due to population starvation and incompatible cross-instance parent selection. We demonstrate that the advantage of MT-EAX derives from increased diversity through parallel search in early generations, which can be successfully preserved using a decoupled configuration to strictly outperform or match standard EAX performance at final convergence.

title: Learning to Solve Complex Constrained Routing Problems with Feasibility-Guided Reward And Diversity-Guided Policy
abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) has achieved remarkable progress in solving routing problems using deep reinforcement learning, yet its application to complex constrained routing problems is still at an early stage. Recent advances have successfully applied Lagrange multiplier variants to handle constraints, but still suffer from limitations in reward configuration and sufficient diversity in exploring, leading to high infeasibility rates and suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose a feasibility-guided reward and diversity-guided policy (FRDP) framework that explicitly targets both enhancing feasibility and promoting exploration diversity. Specifically, FRDP introduces a specialized reward mechanism that differentiates feasible from infeasible solutions, ensuring correct reward ordering and guiding the model toward feasible regions. In parallel, the diversity-guided policy encourages the exploration of varied solution patterns. We evaluated FRDP on two challenging constrained routing problems: the traveling salesman problem with time windows (TSPTW) and the traveling salesman problem with draft limits (TSPDL). Experimental results demonstrate that FRDP significantly improves both solution quality and feasibility over existing neural methods, highlighting its effectiveness in handling complex constrained routing problems. Additional details and supplementary experiments are provided in the appendix, available at: https://zenodo.org/records/19162589.

title: Linear Ordering Problem: Time for a Change
abstract: The Linear Ordering Problem (LOP) is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem with important applications in areas such as economics, social choice, and machine learning. Its most prominent use is the triangulation of economic input-output tables, which helps identify critical industries in an economy. Most existing algorithms have been evaluated on benchmarks derived from outdated macroeconomic data, which no longer reflect the structure of contemporary economies. Furthermore, LOP instances often exhibit many distinct global optima that can differ substantially from one another, creating challenges for applications that rely on a single solution. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel benchmark suite derived from up-to-date real-world economic data and an algorithmic scheme that leverages state-of-the-art LOP metaheuristics to generate diverse sets of high-quality solutions, together with metrics for assessing both quality and diversity. Experiments were conducted to report results on the proposed benchmark suite under both the traditional single-solution setting and the newly introduced multi-solution scenario.

title: Parallel Local Search for MaxSAT with Solutions and Score Functions Co-evolving
abstract: The Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMS) problem is a classical problem that generalizes the fundamental Satisfiability (SAT) problem and has many applications. Local search is an important class of algorithms for computing high-quality solutions to combinatorial optimization problems. Although there has been much progress in serial local search algorithms for the WPMS problem, research on parallel local search algorithms for WPMS remains to be explored. We develop a parallel local search framework for WPMS to leverage the power of parallelism with co-evolving solutions and score functions to improve search efficiency. Based on this parallel framework, we develop the first parallel local search WPMS solver, ParMaxSAT, by plugging in the efficient serial WPMS local search algorithm NuWLS. Experiments demonstrate the efficiency of our solver and the effectiveness of our techniques.

title: SAT-Based Search for Minwise Independent Families
abstract: Optimal minwise independent families of permutations are combinatorial structures designed to realize a large set of highly symmetric monotonicity patterns while using as few permutations as possible. Such families play a central role in efficient Jaccard similarity estimation and related applications in document analysis and machine learning. While practical variants often tolerate slight relaxations of their attributes, we focus on the computational construction of minwise independent families in their pure form. We introduce a constraint-based framework that (i) provides a direct SAT encoding of the underlying combinatorial conditions and (ii) extends a heuristic by Mathon and van Trung to guide the search within this constrained space. Our results show that this hybrid approach is effective in discovering new, provably optimal families and yields substantial speed-ups compared to previous methods. The framework also offers structural insights into these combinatorial objects and supports them with certified optimality proofs.

title: Stein Variational Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Combinatorial black-box optimization in complex and rugged settings demands a careful trade-off between exploiting promising regions of the search space and preserving sufficient exploration to identify multiple optima. Although Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms (EDAs) provide a powerful model-based framework, they often concentrate on a single region of interest, which may result in premature convergence when facing complex or multimodal objective landscapes. In this work, we incorporate the Stein operator to introduce a repulsive mechanism among particles in the parameter space, thereby encouraging the population to disperse and jointly explore several modes of the fitness landscape. Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmark problems show that the proposed method achieves performance competitive with, and in several cases superior to, leading state-of-the-art approaches, particularly on the larger evaluated instances. These findings highlight the potential of Stein variational gradient descent as a promising direction for addressing large, computationally expensive, discrete black-box optimization problems.

title: The Suffering Salesperson
abstract: The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) is a fundamental problem with widespread relevance in modern applications such as parcel delivery. Still, the factors that determine instance difficulty for state-of-the-art TSP solvers, such as LKH and EAX, remain insufficiently understood. Prior work has focused on constructing instances that are challenging for either of the two solvers based on the runtime required by LKH or EAX, respectively, for finding the optimal tour of the instance. However, such measures do not adequately capture the anytime behavior of heuristic algorithms. To address this limitation, we introduce weighted Anytime Runtime Performance (wARP), a novel measure which explicitly accounts for the progression of solution quality over time. An analysis of instances considered difficult by established criteria reveals their diverse anytime behaviors, ranging from instances where solvers quickly find near-optimal tours to instances where near-optimal tours are not found. These patterns can be captured by the new wARP measure. Leveraging the sensitivity of wARP, we propose a gradual instance generation process that constructs instances that are consistently challenging for both LKH and EAX. This provides an alternative basis for evaluating algorithmic variants and enables a more nuanced analysis of their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, the proposed concept is transferable to other domains, providing a foundation for more informative benchmarking and targeted instance generation beyond the TSP.

title: Equilibrium Analysis of a Variable Metric Evolution Strategy
abstract: We study the expected one-step dynamics of a simplified rank-\(\mu \) CMA-ES on the two-dimensional sphere in normal form, with emphasis on the highly anisotropic limit \(\kappa \rightarrow \infty \). In this regime, selection collapses to a one-dimensional truncation geometry, making the dynamics analytically tractable. We derive explicit stationarity conditions for covariance adaptation and step-size adaptation and show that both are governed by the same reduced scaling variable \(s=\sqrt{2}\cos (\alpha )/\sigma \), so that the corresponding stationary thresholds depend only on the selection rate \(\rho \). We then analyze the equilibrium of the normalized step-size in normal form and interpret it as a self-similar stationary regime in which the canonical relation between distance to the optimum and effective step-size is restored in expectation after one update and renormalization. Our analysis isolates a tractable extreme of CMA-ES and clarifies the interaction of covariance adaptation, step-size adaptation, and normal-form renormalization near stationarity.

title: A Generator for Creating Streaming Continuous Optimisation Benchmarks
abstract: In many real-world scenarios, instances arrive in a stream whose characteristics change over time, i.e. the stream is subject to data-drift. The ability to detect and respond to drift is crucial to optimise performance over the stream. However, there is currently no suitable stream-generator on which to evaluate the aforementioned methods. We address this by proposing SCOBench: a fully configurable generator that can generate streams of instances with different drift patterns specified by the user. In contrast to existing stream generators that define drift as a shift in the location of the optima over time of a single instance, SCOBench generates a stream of new instances from multiple functions, while drift between consecutive instances can be defined according to a change in three different metrics (landscape features, probing-trajectories and optima location). We verify that SCOBench correctly generates the intended drift patterns, then demonstrate that algorithms perform differently over streams, highlighting the need for drift detection and algorithm-selection per instance. SCOBench is fully integrated with IOHexperimenter for ease of use. All code and documentation are available as open-source.

title: Combinatorial Landscape Analysis for Dominating Set and Vertex Coloring
abstract: We analyze the two combinatorial problems of Dominating Set and Vertex Coloring regarding what kind of local optima are present for various instances. For a variety of graph classes each, we determine whether the induced landscapes are unimodal, plateau-unimodal (all optima are just one plateau), equimodal (all local optima are global) or truly multimodal. We do this for two different neighborhood operators, one based on making only a single change and one also allowing swaps (interchanging two parts of the solution).

title: Decomposing Anytime Algorithm Performance with Bayesian Ranking ANOVA
abstract: Comparing multiple optimization algorithms across problem instances involves understanding not only which algorithm is best on average, but how instance characteristics shift relative performance over time. The PolarBear framework identifies Pareto-optimal anytime algorithms via scale-free Bayesian ranking models, but pools all instances into a single marginal comparison, discarding structure that could inform algorithm selection at deployment. We extend its temporal Plackett-Luce model with an ANOVA decomposition of latent utilities: algorithm performance over time is decomposed into a global baseline, main effects of instance characteristics, and their interactions, all modeled as time-varying processes. Factor levels are explicitly modeled independently, making the decomposition an analytical tool rather than a predictive model. We develop a diagnostic toolkit for the fitted posterior: Shapley information values quantify the decision-theoretic gain from learning each factor, log-lifts reveal how each factor level shifts performance ratings relative to the global baseline, and conditional anytime Pareto sets identify specialist algorithms that emerge under specific conditions. We demonstrate the framework on the BBOB benchmark suite, decomposing anytime performance of a diverse algorithm portfolio into effects of function identity and dimensionality. Clustering the level-specific deviations from the global baseline produces a data-driven problem taxonomy grounded in algorithmic performance rather than landscape properties.

title: From Networks to Landscapes: Sampling and Topographic Visualisation of Continuous LONs
abstract: Local Optima Networks (LONs) are established graph-based models for landscape analysis, yet their methodological maturity in continuous optimisation lags behind their combinatorial counterparts. This study investigates the challenges of constructing LONs for the Black-Box Optimisation Benchmark (BBOB) suite using a basin-hopping framework. We first identify a critical sampling anomaly—spurious local optima on theoretically unimodal functions—and suggest that vanishing gradients are the primary cause, proposing specific parameters to mitigate this behaviour. To improve high-dimensional interpretability, we introduce an integrated topographic visualisation that superimposes the LON graph onto a reconstructed fitness surface. This approach extends the intuition of 2d heatmaps to higher dimensions, capturing both connectivity and topography. Finally, we characterise the 5d BBOB suite using an expanded set of LON features. Comparative analysis reveals that LON-derived metrics outperform traditional landscape features for 3 of the 4 optimisers tested, suggesting that graph-based models capture structural nuances distinct from traditional metrics. These results contribute to establish the LON framework as a complementary quantitative and visualisation tool to characterise continuous optimisation landscapes.

title: Generating Point Sets of Low Star Discrepancy by Optimizing Kronecker Constructions
abstract: The \(L_{\infty }\) star discrepancy of a point set is a measure for how uniformly a point set is distributed in a given space. Point sets of low star discrepancy are used as designs of experiments, as initial designs for Bayesian optimization algorithms, for quasi-Monte Carlo integration methods, and many other applications. Recent work has shown that classical constructions such as Sobol’, Halton, or Hammersley sequences can be outperformed by large margins when considering point sets of fixed sizes rather than their asymptotic behavior when the number of points tends to infinity. These results, highly relevant to the aforementioned applications, raise the question of how much existing constructions can be improved through size-specific optimization. In this work, we study this question for the 3-dimensional setting, focusing on how well the so-called Kronecker construction performs for various set sizes n. We show that, for settings with at least 500 points, optimizing the two configurable parameters of its construction using evolutionary computation approaches such as CMA-ES yields point sets whose discrepancy values outperform those of the previously best-known sets. Using the algorithm configuration technique Irace, we then derive parameters that yield new state-of-the-art discrepancy values for whole ranges of set sizes. An investigation of the problem landscapes using exploratory landscape analysis reveals that the problem is highly multimodal and that some of its characteristics differ substantially from the 24 BBOB functions.

title: Reshaping the Fitness Landscape of Classification Rule Mining for Clinical Natural Language Processing
abstract: Clinical texts are valuable sources of patient information, but they are hard to process automatically due to synonyms, abbreviations, and terminological variability. Classification rule mining can extract readable “IF-THEN” rules that clinicians can understand and verify. Standard evolutionary rule miners rely on exact word matching, which fails when the same concept is expressed with different words (e.g., “renal failure” vs. “kidney failure”). This fragments the fitness landscape into vast neutral plateaus where standard operators cannot progress.We propose a multi-objective evolutionary framework that integrates word embeddings into binary classification rule mining at two levels: soft matching, which allows semantically similar terms to contribute to rule coverage during fitness evaluation, and a semantic mutation operator, which replaces terms with embedding-space neighbors during search. Together, these components restore a continuous optimization gradient in place of the flat landscape caused by terminological variability.Experiments on MIMIC-IV-Note across five diagnostic targets show that our framework more than doubles the mean hypervolume (+116%) and substantially improves the F1-score (+80%) compared to exact-matching baseline NSGA-II and bitflip mutation, while maintaining fully interpretable rule structures. Fitness landscape analysis confirms that the combined approach reduces neutrality and increases information content, explaining its superior search dynamics.

title: Sampling on Random Subspaces Under Limited Data in the Context of Exploratory Landscape Analysis
abstract: Classical space-filling designs often fail to provide reliable statistical results for Exploratory Landscape Analysis (ELA) when only limited evaluation budgets are available, as commonly occurs in high-dimensional problems or other resource-constrained settings, resulting in noisy and unstable landscape descriptors.To address this challenge, we propose an alternative sampling strategy for ELA based on random linear embeddings. Rather than sampling uniformly in the full decision space, we allocate the budget to randomly oriented low-dimensional subspaces and investigate whether this improves the robustness of the resulting landscape descriptors.We compare full-space and embedding-based sampling strategies across several classical ELA feature sets on the noiseless Black-Box Optimization Benchmarking (BBOB) test suite from the COmparing Continuous Optimizers (COCO) environment, in a 20-dimensional setting. Our results suggest that random linear embeddings constitute a promising alternative for budget-constrained ELA, although their effectiveness remains dependent on the feature class and the underlying problem.

title: The Traveling Thief Problem with Time Windows: Benchmarks and Heuristics
abstract: While traditional optimization problems were often studied in isolation, many real-world problems today require interdependence among multiple optimization components. The traveling thief problem (TTP) is a multi-component problem whose components are interdependent and has been widely studied in the literature. In this paper, we introduce and investigate the TTP with time window constraints which provides a TTP variant highly relevant to real-world situations where good can only be collected at given time intervals. We examine adaptions of existing approaches for TTP and the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) with time windows to this new problem and evaluate their performance. Furthermore, we provide a new heuristic approach for the TTP with time windows. To evaluate algorithms for TTP with time windows, we introduce new TTP benchmark instances with time windows based on TTP instances existing in the literature. Our experimental investigations evaluate the different approaches and show that the newly designed algorithm outperforms the other approaches on a wide range of benchmark instances.

title: Untangling the Tapestry: k-Bounded Problems and Local Optima Networks
abstract: Local optima networks (LONs) have recently been used to analyse subfunction structure in problems which contain strong linkage. However, many questions remain: for example, it is not known how LON subfunction structure relates to optimiser performance on the underlying problems. In addition, the potential of using the associated features to distinguish between classes of problem is not well understood. Therefore we address these gaps. We construct LONs in two different ways, propose a new set of features (which are based upon the structure of subfunction argument sets), and investigate the associations with performance of three state-of-the-art optimisers. The results indicate that the subfunction-related features may depend on the LON construction algorithm and that some of them are useful for separating problem classes. Also, the proposed features seem to relate to the performance of some optimisers for some problem-operator combinations. The approach and the findings together not only provide new insight about the interplay between the studied problems and optimisers, but also lay the groundwork for possible online LON-based operator adaptation in the future.

title: Improved Runtime Bound for the $$(\mu +1)\text {-EA}$$ on BinVal
abstract: We study the \((\mu +1)\) EA on the Binary Value function BinVal. We show that it needs at most \(O(\mu \log \mu \cdot n \log n)\) function evaluations to find the optimum when \(\mu = o(n/\log n)\). This substantially improves upon the recent upper bound of \(O(\mu ^5 n \log (n/\mu ^4))\) by Krejca, Neumann and Witt. Our results hold for several mutation operators including standard bit mutation. In particular, our bound implies that the \((\mu +1)\) EA is at most a factor \(O(\log \mu \cdot \log n)\) slower on BinVal than on OneMax.

title: Never-Forgetting Genetic Algorithms on OneMax: First Insights
abstract: One possible, but rarely used way of managing populations in evolutionary algorithms is to never discard solutions and let the population grow, which puts much more emphasis on selection operators. A recent work proposed a particular framework for that, called never-forgetting genetic algorithms, and showed experimentally that it has noticeable benefits in terms of the expected number of evaluations until the optimum is hit on a number of pseudo-Boolean optimisation problems of theoretical importance. The working principles, however, were not understood well.In this work, we make first important steps towards such an understanding by combined means of runtime analysis and experimental insights. These include proven recommendations for the mutation operator parameters following from some lower bounds on the runtime, experimental confirmation of importance of selection mechanisms, a strong indication that requiring a stochastically sampled minimum distance between crossover parents is crucial, and few insights into the structure of the population.

title: On the Generalization Bounds of Symbolic Regression with Genetic Programming
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) with genetic programming (GP) aims to discover interpretable mathematical expressions directly from data. Despite its strong empirical success, the theoretical understanding of why GP-based SR generalizes beyond the training data remains limited. In this work, we provide a learning-theoretic analysis of SR models represented as expression trees. We derive a generalization bound for GP-style SR under constraints on tree size, depth, and learnable constants. Our result decomposes the generalization gap into two interpretable components: a structure-selection term, reflecting the combinatorial complexity of choosing an expression-tree structure, and a constant-fitting term, capturing the complexity of optimizing numerical constants within a fixed structure. This decomposition provides a theoretical perspective on several widely used practices in GP, including parsimony pressure, depth limits, numerically stable operators, and interval arithmetic. In particular, our analysis shows how structural restrictions reduce hypothesis-class growth while stability mechanisms control the sensitivity of predictions to parameter perturbations. By linking these practical design choices to explicit complexity terms in the generalization bound, our work offers a principled explanation for commonly observed empirical behaviors in GP-based SR and contributes towards a more rigorous understanding of its generalization properties.

title: On the Runtime Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Hyper-Heuristics
abstract: Selection Hyper-heuristics (HHs) automate algorithmic design by selecting from a set of low-level heuristics which one to apply at each stage of the optimisation process. Several impressive results have been recently rigorously proven regarding the performance of selection hyper-heuristics (HHs) for standard benchmark functions. However, the learning mechanisms employed by these HHs are considerably simplified compared to the machine learning techniques typically used in real world applications. In this paper we analyse a Reinforcement Learning Hyper-heuristic (RLHH) from the literature. The only previous result available proved that for a wide range of parameter settings, RLHH does not learn to select heuristics appropriately for the standard \(\textsc {LeadingOnes}\) benchmark function. In this paper, we rigorously prove that with appropriate parameter values RLHH equipped with two random local search operators, \(\textsc {RLS}_1\) and \(\textsc {RLS}_2\) optimises the \(\textsc {LeadingOnes}\) benchmark function in the best possible expected runtime achievable with the two operators up to lower order terms. Experiments show that for realistic problem sizes it is faster than the Generalised Random Gradient HH which was previously proven to also have optimal expected runtime up to lower order terms.

title: Runtime Analysis of the $$(\mu + 1)$$ -ES in a Homogenous Progress Model
abstract: We introduce a new simple model to study the fitness progress of Evolution Strategies (ES) in generic problems. In this model, we bypass the underlying fitness landscape and assume that the mutation of any individual produces an offspring whose fitness relative to the parent is given by an invariant distribution Z, such as a mean-shifted Gaussian. This serves as a prototypical model for the optimisation landscape when an evolution algorithm operates far from the global optimum. This simple model can be used to approximate the optimisation process for problems where it is intractable to model the exact fitness function, including tasks such as hyperparameter tuning in machine learning models.We rigorously analyse the expected growth rate \(\mathcal {R}_{\mu }\) of the continuous steady-state \((\mu +1)\)-ES in this model. Unlike comma-selection strategies, the steady-state \((\mu +1)\)-ES maintains overlapping generations, introducing complex mathematical dependencies among surviving parents that make it harder to analyse. We give a general technique to analyse the \((\mu +1)\)-ES by constructing modified processes whose growth rates provably sandwich that of the original process. These modified processes are then easier to analyse but still close enough to the true process to give a tight bound on the expected growth rate. When \(Z = \mathcal {N}(-\delta , 1)\) and \(\mu \le e^{\delta }\), we show that \(\mathcal {R}_{\mu } = \frac{\log ^{1 + o(1)} \mu }{\mu } \mathcal {R}_1\).

title: Automated Construction of Algorithm Portfolios with Iterated Racing
abstract: Automated algorithm configuration methods such as irace are typically designed to identify a single high-performing configuration. However, in heterogeneous-instance settings, different configurations may perform well on different subsets of problem instances, so a portfolio of configurations can be a more appropriate target than a single one. This is especially relevant when multiple solver runs can be executed in parallel. In this paper, we propose Portfolio-irace (P-irace), an extension of irace that returns a portfolio of user-defined cardinality and jointly optimises its members within a single iterated racing process. Candidate portfolios are evaluated and eliminated as portfolio-level objects, rather than being formed only after racing or constructed sequentially across stages. We compare P-irace with Best-k irace, which forms a portfolio post hoc from the top-k configurations returned by a standard irace run, and with a Hydra-irace baseline, which constructs portfolios sequentially. Experiments on a synthetic benchmark with complementary optima and on diverse instances of the quadratic assignment problem show that P-irace consistently constructs stronger portfolios than Best-k irace. Compared with Hydra-irace, its advantage is most pronounced under limited configuration budgets, while the two methods become closer as the budget increases. These results suggest that, for the settings considered in this paper, portfolio-level joint racing is a budget-effective alternative to post hoc selection and a competitive alternative to sequential portfolio construction.

title: RL-Exponential-DAS: Exponential Decision Schedules for Dynamic Algorithm Selection
abstract: Dynamic Algorithm Selection (DAS) in meta-black-box optimization is fundamentally constrained when the underlying optimizer portfolio is structurally heterogeneous: switching between optimizers with incompatible internal states disrupts the adaptive mechanisms on which late-stage convergence critically depends. Prior reinforcement-learning-based DAS methods largely sidestep this difficulty by restricting selection to portfolios drawn from a single algorithmic family. We revisit DAS from a complementary standpoint and investigate whether the temporal placement of selection decisions, rather than their content alone, constitutes an exploitable axis of design. We introduce RL-Exponential-DAS, a PPO-based framework in which decision checkpoints follow an exponentially increasing schedule, inducing frequent early interventions and progressively longer uninterrupted optimization intervals as the search matures. The framework is coupled with a memory-handling mechanism that admits selection over a structurally heterogeneous portfolio comprising G3PCX, SPSO, and LMCMAES, whose internal states admit no common representation. On the noiseless BBOB benchmark, exponential scheduling yields statistically significant AOCC improvements over uniform scheduling in dimensions \(D \in \{5,10\}\). A policy-level analysis reveals an interpretable exploration-to-exploitation structure that sharpens with dimensionality: early checkpoints are dominated by SPSO-driven exploration, while late checkpoints concentrate mass on LMCMAES.

title: SAFAS: Simulated Algorithm Feature-Enhanced Automated Algorithm Selection for Black-Box Optimization
abstract: Automated algorithm selection for continuous black-box optimization depends on instance representations that are both informative and affordable. Existing approaches usually rely on either problem feature-based representations or problem–algorithm interaction features. The former are reusable and portfolio-independent, but they do not directly characterize algorithm behavior on the target instance. The latter can be highly informative, but they often introduce substantial runtime overhead and scale poorly as the algorithm portfolio grows. In this paper, we propose a Simulated Algorithm Feature-enhanced Automated Algorithm Selection (SAFAS) framework that connects these two perspectives through a shared sampling budget. SAFAS extracts problem features from shared space-filling evaluation samples, fits a surrogate model of the target problem, and derives simulated algorithm features by running candidate algorithms on the surrogate instead of the original objective. The same sampled data therefore support both problem characterization and instance-dependent behavior modeling. To further reduce inference cost, we also propose predictive SAF, which predicts a selectively aggregated simulated algorithm-feature vector from sampled-response observations on the shared design without explicitly executing the full portfolio at test time. Experiments on the black-box optimization benchmarking suite across multiple portfolio sizes and problem dimensions show that explicit SAF consistently improves or matches strong problem feature-based baselines, while predictive SAF yields substantial speedups but remains clearly weaker than explicit SAF in predictive quality.

title: Theory-Guided Online Algorithm Selection: Benchmarking Algorithm Switching for Pseudo-boolean Optimization
abstract: Online algorithm selection (OAS) is a meta-optimization technique that switches between different algorithms during the optimization process. In contrast to online parameter control, which adapts components in a given algorithm, OAS can make more extensive changes, including switching to algorithms from different families. A recent theoretical study by Antipov and Doerr (GECCO 2026) showed that even a single switch can yield an asymptotical speedup on OneMax when combining the \((1 + 1)\) EA and the \((1 + (\lambda , \lambda ))\) GA. In this paper, we show that their theoretical insights extend to a much broader class of problems, including OneMax variants, LeadingOnes and some MAX-3SAT instances. We show that the \((1 + 1)\) EA tends to work well in the early stages of optimization, while the \((1 + (\lambda , \lambda ))\) GA is more efficient when it comes closer to the optimum. Based on this, we benchmark an OAS approach that switches between these optimizers. We observe that parameters of this OAS, such as the optimal population size and the stagnation detection threshold (which triggers the switching between algorithms), differ between the considered problems. However, we manage to identify well-performing settings for the majority of considered cases, showing that OAS outperforms its component algorithms on a broader range of problems than just the theoretically analyzed OneMax. These findings reinforce the benefits of OAS and motivate further study of the phase-dependent efficiency of evolutionary algorithms.

title: Unsupervised Multi-Kernel Learning for Automated Algorithm Selection
abstract: Automated algorithm selection in black-box optimization typically relies on supervised models that map landscape features to algorithm performance labels. Such models are costly to train, benchmark-dependent, and often fail to generalize to unseen problem classes. We study an unsupervised alternative: multi-kernel clustering over heterogeneous landscape representations, in which problem instances are grouped without using performance labels in the clustering stage, and the resulting clusters are mapped post hoc to solver recommendations through a strictly separated three-stage evaluation protocol. Drawing on two decades of advances in multiple kernel learning, we adopt a multi-kernel k-means formulation that jointly learns cluster assignments and kernel weights over four heterogeneous landscape views: ELA, DeepELA, DoE2Vec, and TransOptAS. On affine BBOB-derived selector tasks for Differential Evolution (DE) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) at a fixed evaluation budget, we report mean±standard-deviation selector profiles over 50 independent random seeds for stochastic configurations. Multi-kernel clustering obtains the strongest mean profile on the DE portfolio and remains competitive with, and nominally ahead of, the leading baselines on the more compressed PSO portfolio, where differences among the best methods are small relative to stochastic variation. In representative median-seed runs used for visualization, the learned kernel weights retain ELA and TransOptAS while assigning zero weight to DeepELA and DoE2Vec, providing a task-specific interpretation of which representations are retained by the multi-kernel model for selector-oriented grouping.

title: When Does Parameter Control Pay Off?
abstract: In low-dimensional (D=2–10), micro-budget (\(\le \)5000 function evaluations) BBOB optimization, we investigate when adaptive parameter control amortizes its learning cost against tuned static baselines. Evaluating a four-level algorithm complexity ladder (Fixed ES, Adaptive ES, sep-CMA-ES, CMA-ES) across 24 BBOB functions with 2,382 problem instances, we find that step-size control alone barely exceeds break-even (PBE=52%), while diagonal covariance adaptation (sep-CMA-ES) provides the largest marginal gain (PBE=70%), and full CMA-ES adaptation reaches 79% (95% bootstrap CI: [78%, 81%]). The per-level analysis reveals that sep-CMA-ES is the most cost-effective adaptation level: it captures the largest performance jump at O(D) cost. High-conditioning functions favor adaptation (PBE=94%), while weak-structure functions show marginal benefit (62%). A negative finding emerges: zero-cost metadata features cannot predict the oracle-optimal algorithm level, and the simple “always CMA-ES” policy outperforms ML-based selectors. These findings are specific to the ES family and BBOB suite; generalization to other algorithm families and benchmarks is important future work.

title: Benchmarking Zero-Shot LLM-Generated Parent Selection in Genetic Programming for Symbolic Regression
abstract: Parent selection significantly affects exploration, exploitation, and complexity control in genetic programming (GP) for symbolic regression. It is unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can synthesize effective operators in a zero-shot setting without iterative meta-evolution. Here, zero-shot means that the model receives only the task description, with no reference operators or iterative feedback. In this work, we benchmark zero-shot synthesis of parent-selection operators across eight LLMs within a standard GP framework for symbolic regression. Each model receives the same natural-language prompt to generate a parent-selection operator, which is then evaluated in a standard GP framework with only the parent-selection operator replaced, while all other components and the evolutionary-search budget are held constant. For each LLM, ten independent zero-shot operators are evaluated on twelve OpenML regression benchmarks and compared against automatic lexicase and tournament selection baselines. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro stand out for consistently strong performance on both training and held-out test \(R^2\). The strongest operator in our benchmark—a Kimi K2.5 zero-shot synthesis—surpasses the automatic lexicase and tournament baselines in search effectiveness. These results suggest that zero-shot LLM synthesis is a viable approach to generating competitive GP selection operators. Analysis shows that many generated operators use semantics to guide selection, suggesting that LLMs can produce non-trivial search heuristics from the task description alone. We also examine the relationship between public LLM leaderboard rankings and GP performance. Widely used benchmarks, such as Humanity’s Last Exam and SWE-bench Verified, strongly correlate with training \(R^2\), while their relationship to held-out test \(R^2\) is weaker and less clear.

title: BERT Mutation for Genetic Algorithms: A Deep Transformer Operator
abstract: Traditional genetic algorithm mutation strategies typically apply stochastic gene modifications without considering broader genomic context or learning from historical evolutionary data. To address this, we introduce BERT Mutation for Genetic Algorithms (GAs), a novel, domain-independent contextual mutation operator that adapts the Transformer architecture to fixed-length genetic representations. While deep learning-based operators have shown success in Genetic Programming, extending them to GAs is challenged by “semantic opacity”—the lack of explicit structural definitions in linear integer or binary vectors. To overcome this, we propose a novel data augmentation strategy that generates pseudo-training examples derived from the population’s elite. This strategy enriches the training signal by constructing augmented trajectories toward high-fitness solutions, stabilizing the reinforcement learning process. We evaluate the operator across four diverse domains: Frozen Lake, Artificial Ant, Graph Coloring, and Unweighted Set Cover.Our results demonstrate that BERT Mutation consistently outperforms traditional stochastic operators (One-Point, Uniform, and Zigzag) and an adaptive operator (AOS) in both convergence speed and final solution quality. Notably, BERT Mutation achieves superior average fitness in approximately half the wall-clock time and fewer than half the generations required by competing baselines. Furthermore, diversity analysis confirms that BERT Mutation preserves structured, meaningful population diversity, avoiding the premature convergence seen in simpler operators.

title: Designing Hypervolume Subset Selection Algorithms with Large Language Models
abstract: Hypervolume subset selection (HSS) aims to select a subset from a candidate solution set that maximizes hypervolume. HSS is challenging because hypervolume evaluation is computationally expensive and the contribution of each solution depends on the other selected solutions, making effective HSS heuristic design nontrivial. Recent advances in large language models (LLM) based automatic heuristic design (AHD), including MEoH for multi-objective heuristic search, suggest a promising direction for addressing such challenges. However, existing LLM-based AHD frameworks struggle to generate competitive HSS heuristics. To this end, we propose HSS-MEoH, the first multi-objective LLM-based AHD framework for HSS. HSS-MEoH incorporates three mechanisms: 1) Diverse Warm-Start Initialization, which forms the initial population using a set of human-designed representative HSS heuristics; 2) Reflective Evolution Mechanism, which enables the LLM to summarize search experience and generate offspring in more promising directions; and 3) Novelty-Weighted Parent Selection, which determines parent selection probabilities based on both heuristic performance and prior selection frequency to favor less frequently selected heuristics. Experimental results show that HSS-MEoH achieves better trade-offs between solution quality and runtime than MEoH and produces a more diverse set of non-dominated heuristics. Moreover, HSS-MEoH outperforms most state-of-the-art human-designed heuristics across diverse HSS problem instances. Code is available at https://github.com/MOL-SZU/HSS-MEoH.

title: Large Language Models for the Automatic Design of Memetic Algorithms
abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems are standard benchmarks in the field, and memetic algorithms are popular tools for designing high-performing methods to solve them. Designing efficient memetic algorithms requires substantial manual effort and relies heavily on experience. In this work, we implement memetic algorithms as compositions of interchangeable components encoded by a context-free grammar that can be automatically configured. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) suggest they can assist algorithm designers by improving implementation efficiency. We analyze the execution efficiency of LLM-generated code compared to manual implementations written by a programmer familiar with optimization algorithms. The analysis considers operators such as initialization, mutation, crossover, selection, and local search for permutation-based combinatorial optimization problems. Results show that, while the manual implementations are often efficient, the iterative LLM refinement consistently produces faster code. Although these implementations significantly improve execution efficiency, they may reduce code readability. This underscores the need for an effective methodology for LLM-assisted algorithm design, including a validation process to ensure interface compatibility, preserve the intended algorithmic structure and semantics, and detect unintended behavioral deviations.

title: Multi-objective Coevolution of Prompts and Templates for Circuit Approximation
abstract: Approximate multipliers deliberately relax computational accuracy to achieve gains in power efficiency, latency, and silicon area, which makes them well-suited for error-resilient applications such as neural networks. In this work, we introduce a co-evolutionary algorithm that leverages an off-the-shelf large language model (LLM) without requiring domain-specific training to automate the design of optimized 8-bit approximate multipliers. The approach simultaneously evolves a population of candidate circuits and a population of prompt templates that steer LLM-driven modifications. Experimental results for several target design objectives demonstrate that the proposed method discovers approximate multipliers with improved error–area trade-offs compared to highly optimized circuits from the EvoApproxLib library.

title: Evolutionary Bilevel Reward Shaping for Generalization in Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) often suffers from performance degradation when deployed in environments that differ from those encountered during training. Existing techniques such as domain randomization (DR) mitigate this, but require access to diverse training environments and full trajectory observability, assumptions that fail in privacy-preserving or restricted scenarios where only scalar performance metrics are available. We propose Generalization via Evolutionary Reward Shaping (GERS), a bilevel optimization approach to improve generalization on unseen test environments using only scalar feedback from validation environments. At the lower level, an RL agent guided via a reward function shaped by the upper level learns a policy on a limited set of training environments with accessible trajectory data; at the upper level, CMA-ES optimizes the reward shaping parameters to maximize the cumulative unshaped reward on separate validation environments for which trajectory access is unavailable. Results on continuous control tasks indicate that GERS outperforms the standard RL baseline on unseen test environments. GERS performance is comparable to DR, despite DR treating the combined set of training and validation environments of GERS as a single training set that requires trajectory access, whereas GERS cannot access validation trajectories. These results confirm that GERS effectively enhances generalization under restricted data access constraints.

title: PAEvo: Plan-Algorithm Evolution with LLMs for Automatic Heuristic Design
abstract: Handcrafting heuristics is a common approach for solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, but it typically requires substantial domain knowledge and manual effort. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), with their strong reasoning and code generation capabilities, have made LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design (AHD) a promising paradigm for reducing the reliance on expertise in heuristic development. However, existing methods often rely on single-step heuristic generation and fail to preserve useful insights discovered during the search process, limiting their effectiveness on complex problems. To address these limitations, we propose a plan-algorithm evolution framework (PAEvo) that integrates explicit planning with evolutionary search. PAEvo models high-level plans as evolutionary individuals and co-evolves them with heuristic algorithms, enabling LLMs to iteratively refine structured solution strategies while generating executable heuristics. In addition, a self-collaboration mechanism is introduced in which multiple LLM roles jointly perform plan evolution and heuristic evolution. The evolved plans not only guide the generation of higher-quality heuristics for complex problems but also improve interpretability by explicitly representing the heuristic design logic. Experiments on multiple NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems show that PAEvo consistently outperforms existing LLM-based AHD methods.

title: Reinforcement Learning Enhanced LLM Agents for Complex Vehicle Routing Problems
abstract: Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) are fundamental combinatorial optimization problems with widespread applications in various scenarios. The advanced optimization solvers can effectively solve such problems. However, modeling complex VRP variants for solvers often requires substantial domain expertise, which limits the accessibility of advanced optimization technologies. In this paper, we propose Reinforcement Learning Enhanced LLM Agents (RLEA), a multi-agent framework designed to automate the modeling of complex VRPs. RLEA introduces a lightweight neural Planner trained with Soft Q-learning to efficiently orchestrate the actions of LLM-based agents. In addition, we equip the system with an evolutionary memory module and retrieval-augmented generation, enabling the agent to leverage both accumulated experience and external solver knowledge during program generation and refinement for solving VRPs. We evaluated 48 distinct VRP variants across various solvers. The experimental results demonstrate that RLEA outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method, achieving a 16.67% higher success rate while significantly reducing runtime errors. These results validate that integrating reinforcement learning with LLM-based reasoning is highly effective for automated optimization modeling. The appendix is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19134435.

title: AutoEJS: Efficient and Effective Joint Hyperparameter and Architecture Search
abstract: Neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization are critical for improving deep neural network performance. However, existing approaches typically treat them as isolated problems or optimize them sequentially, ignoring the intrinsic coupling between architectures and hyperparameters. This necessitates a joint hyperparameter and architecture search method. Nevertheless, such joint optimization is highly challenging due to the vast coupled search space and the prohibitive cost of candidate evaluation. To address these challenges, we propose AutoEJS, an efficient and effective three-stage hybrid iterative optimization framework for joint search. First, we utilize a representative proxy dataset for rapid warm-up to identify promising regions efficiently. Second, to overcome the tendency of conventional surrogate-assisted search heuristics to become trapped in local optima, we integrate large language models as semantic explorers to inject diverse, high-potential candidates into the iterative process. Finally, a selective re-evaluation mechanism robustly transfers knowledge to the full dataset, ensuring precise fine-tuning with a minimal budget. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that AutoEJS achieves significantly higher efficiency than advanced iterative optimization heuristics. Moreover, it consistently boosts the accuracy of established network architectures across diverse datasets, yielding improvements of 2.5% on CIFAR-100 and 6.5% on Oxford Flowers. Furthermore, our approach outperforms prior joint search methods in terms of optimization effectiveness.

title: Bio-Inspired Palette Evolution in Indirectly Encoded Substrates: Timescale Compatibility Shapes Activation Function Discovery
abstract: Indirectly encoded neural networks can assign different activation functions to individual nodes, but the right functions are rarely known in advance. When the available set contains only standard monotonic functions, problems like parity become unsolvable, yet an all-inclusive palette underperforms a curated one. How should evolution discover which functions to use? We address this as a meta-learning problem, designing 13 strategies (11 inspired by biological adaptation mechanisms, plus baseline and oracle controls) that modify the set of available activation functions during evolution. Each strategy translates a biological principle into an evolutionary operator: for example, circadian-inspired oscillatory gating cycles functions in and out of the palette on a fixed schedule, while immune-inspired Clonal Selection permanently protects functions that consistently correlate with fitness. We evaluate all strategies across more than 3,000 runs on parity and non-parity problems, first evolving the activation palette alone, then co-evolving a per-node aggregation palette on harder problems; an independent replication with new seeds confirms a stable high-reliability tier, with Circadian holding its top rank. Bio-inspired strategies match the solve rate of a tuned baseline but converge up to twice as fast, with Circadian halving total compute. Strategy rankings reverse across problem types, with no single strategy dominating all domains. Strategy success is largely shaped by timescale compatibility: strategies whose characteristic operating timescale matches the evolutionary evaluation window consistently outperform those that operate too slowly. This gives a practical guideline: match the mechanism’s timescale to the evaluation budget. Rescaling the slowest strategy bypasses the oscillatory barrier entirely: all nine solutions solve parity with non-oscillatory activations paired with min or max aggregation.

title: Building Fairness-Aware Ensembles with AutoFairGE
abstract: Fairness-aware Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) has emerged as a promising method for balancing accuracy and fairness. However, most existing methods focus on single-model generation, overlooking the potential benefits of ensemble learning. This paper extends AutoFairGE, a Multi-Objective Grammatical Evolution-based fairness-aware AutoML, from single-model generation to ensemble construction. We leverage AutoFairGE to jointly optimize the overall ensemble composition, as well as the algorithm selection and hyperparameter configuration of individual base models, to generate a set of Pareto-optimal ensemble models that balance accuracy and fairness. The enriched search space enables exploration of a more diverse set of model configurations. In addition, we adopt the knee point concept to assist decision-makers in evaluating and selecting well-balanced solutions from the Pareto-front. Experimental results show that the proposed ensemble-based method achieves more competitive accuracy-fairness trade-offs.

title: Data Centric AutoML Embedding Optimisation for Mode of Delivery Prediction
abstract: Multimodal learning pipelines increasingly rely on high-dimensional embedding representations extracted from pre-trained models. However, these embedding spaces often contain redundancy and noise, which can hinder the learning process. In this work, we reformulate multimodal learning as a data-centric optimisation problem, where the goal is to jointly optimise feature selection, instance selection and model choice in embedding space. To this end, we adopt the Evolutionary Data-Centric AutoML (EDCA) framework to operate directly over multimodal embeddings, treated as structured data, enabling the automatic search for efficient predictive pipelines. The proposed approach is evaluated on a real-world clinical application for predicting mode of delivery following Induction of Labour (IOL). The multimodal data combines maternal-fetal tabular clinical data and third-trimester ultrasound images. Their embeddings are extracted from a pre-trained multimodal model and organised into multiple configurations, which are then optimised using EDCA. Results show that this approach can achieve comparable average performance to multimodal architectures and occasionally identify better configurations, relying on selected subsets of samples and features, which shows that performance improvements can be driven by data quality rather than model complexity. These findings highlight the effectiveness of EDCA for optimising representations and support its suitability for complex multimodal problems in real-world applications.
