title: Energy-Efficient AI-Assisted Evolution: A Case Study on Minimizing the Power Consumption of Deep Neural Crossover
abstract: Deep-learning-based genetic operators can substantially improve evolutionary search quality, but they also introduce significant computational and energy overhead, bringing the Red AI vs. Green AI tension into evolutionary computation. In this work, we study the energy footprint of Deep Neural Crossover, a reinforcement-learning-based multi-parent crossover operator, and evaluate parameter-level strategies to reduce its power consumption without sacrificing solution quality. We profile experiments with process-level energy measurements and analyze two optimization levers: training batch size and a new fitness-based scheduling threshold that triggers backpropagation only after meaningful fitness improvement. Experiments on benchmark Bin-Packing and Graph Coloring instances show that changing batch size alone has little effect on total energy, whereas the proposed scheduling strategy yields substantial savings. In particular, using larger scheduling thresholds considerably reduces energy consumption while keeping fitness close to the best-performing configurations and, in several cases, matching or improving it. These results provide a practical pathway for greener neuro-evolutionary algorithms through adaptive training schedules.

title: Model Merging to Evolution: Parameter Space Exploration for Expert Models
abstract: Model merging integrates the capabilities of multiple expert models to create strong models for multiple tasks without additional training, thereby reducing computational resource requirements. However, existing methods operate within the convex combination space of expert models, failing to explore high-performance regions outside this space. This paper proposes the MERGEvolve framework, which unifies model merging and evolution within an evolution strategy by treating the merged model as the initialization for evolutionary exploration of the parameter space. During the merging phase, expert models act as deterministic sources to build a strong initial point. The evolution phase then explores the parameter space using random noise. Theoretical analysis shows that MERGEvolve explores regions outside the convex combination space. Extensive experiments on single-task and multi-task benchmarks demonstrate that MERGEvolve consistently achieves performance competitive with advanced model merging baselines. Ablation studies confirm that a high-quality initial point is critical for efficient exploration of the parameter space.

title: NEATWork: A Spatial Network Optimizer
abstract: NASA’s planned sustained presence of humans on the Moon will require significant volumes of icy regolith transport across the lunar surface. Algorithmic planning of efficient spatial transport networks connecting multiple terminals and optimizing across a range of objectives remains an open challenge. To address this problem, we developed NEATWork, a spatial network planner. By modifying the well-known NEAT genetic algorithm—traditionally used for the development of neural networks—we present a graph optimization approach that can take into account various spatial and topological objectives. We illustrate our solution using the case of lunar transport network planning, though it can be easily deployed in other network planning scenarios where spatial cost maps can be made and the flexibility for a black box cost function optimization is of interest. We provide two open-source implementations.

title: NEMESIS: Evolving Real-Time Semantic Segmentation Architectures for Robotics
abstract: Real-time semantic segmentation for robotics is strictly limited by the computational capacity and energy budget of edge devices, usually requiring lightweight architectures that balance accuracy with efficiency. While existing Neuroevolution (NE) research often prioritizes accuracy, this work addresses the gap for architectures that optimize performance alongside throughput and energy efficiency. We propose NEMESIS, a framework to design semantic segmentation networks, that uses flexible encoding for depth-wise separable convolutions, parallel modules, and complex fusion mechanisms (including spatial and channel attention). Using a fitness function that combines performance (Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU)), throughput (FPS) and energy usage (Watt), we validated the approach on the Cityscapes dataset. When deploying the best models discovered by NEMESIS on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin, two architectures achieved real-time performance: a Dual-Branch model reached 28.9 FPS (0.54 mIoU), and a Dual-Branch Dilation achieved 170 FPS (0.50 mIoU), with the latter achieving an over five-fold increase of the throughput of the state-of-the-art PPLiteSeg. These results demonstrate that NEMESIS can autonomously generate viable, efficient architectures for resource-constrained edge computing without extensive human domain expertise.

title: Fast Greedy Selection Hyper-heuristics
abstract: Selection hyper-heuristics (HHs) are self-adaptive algorithms that select from a pre-defined set of low-level heuristics which one to apply at each decision point of the optimisation process. The simple Greedy selection HH works by running all heuristics at the same time and accepting the action from the heuristic that produces the largest improvement in the solution quality. Recent analyses have shown that the performance of the Greedy HH is essentially equivalent to one that chooses heuristics uniformly at random in each iteration, and that a Generalised Greedy HH (GG) that applies the greedily chosen heuristic for an exploitation period of \(\tau >0\) iterations can outperform its low-level heuristics when acting on their own for the LeadingOnes benchmark function, if GG is equipped with two operators. We first prove that the best runtime achievable by GG using two operators is not optimal. Furthermore, we show that GG is ineffective because its performance degrades with the increase of the size of the heuristic set it can select from. To overcome this limitation, we improve the HH by allowing it to apply the greedily chosen heuristic in a gradient descent manner. The new Fast Greedy HH is shown to have optimal performance on the LeadingOnes benchmark function for any constant number of low-level heuristics. The rigorous theoretical results are complemented with an experimental analysis showing the improved performance in practice of the Fast Greedy HH over previously studied HHs for the function.

title: Repopulation Frequency as a Driving Factor in Bias Correction in Asynchronous Parallel Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithms improve computational efficiency but introduce evaluation-time bias: architectures with shorter evaluation times accumulate disproportionate reproductive opportunity, steering the search toward compact but potentially suboptimal solutions. While correction strategies such as Harada’s frequency-based parent selection and SWEET have been proposed, their behavior in island-based neuroevolution systems with periodic repopulation remains uncharacterized. We present a systematic ablation study comparing these bias correction strategies within EXAMM, a distributed asynchronous neuroevolution framework, across six island repopulation frequencies on three real-world time-series datasets: aviation flight recorder data, coal power plant sensor data and wind turbine sensor data. Each of the 24 experimental conditions is evaluated across 10 independent trials with a fixed budget of 10,000 genome evaluations, with statistical significance assessed via the Mann-Whitney U test against a no-repopulation vanilla baseline. Results show that repopulation frequency provides the strongest effect across the evaluated strategies.

title: From Importance Shifts to Landscape Topology: Characterizing and Exploiting Hyperparameter Spaces in Parallel Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Scaling PPO to thousands of parallel environments changes not only training speed but also the structure of the hyperparameter (HP) optimization problem. We study how HP importance and fitness landscape topology change across 37,200 PPO training runs spanning five HP groups, four continuous-control environments, and five parallelism levels (64–1,024 environments). First, using fANOVA on 372,000 evaluation snapshots, we show that HP importance rankings are stable across parallelism levels (\(p > 0.96\) in Friedman tests) but importance magnitudes shift by up to an order of magnitude (the data-collection HP rollout_length alone rises \(10.1\times \) in mean importance from 64 to 1,024 environments), with a consistent stage-wise transition from data-collection to optimization HP dominance. Second, applying GraphFLA to 120 landscape slices, we identify structural correlates: HP landscapes become smoother (local-optima ratio \(-50.5\%\)) yet more globally deceptive (fitness–distance correlation grows more negative with parallelism, \(\rho = -0.27\)), with simpler HP interactions (reciprocal sign epistasis \(-52.9\%\)). Third, we show that landscape topology is associated with differential HPO algorithm performance: a correlation analysis across eight HPO methods and 20 benchmark conditions reveals which landscape properties favor which method family. We present this third contribution as a proof-of-concept. Although a direct feature-based meta-model does not yet beat trivial baselines at this scale, a chapter-conditioned selector that keys on chapter identity, not on the GraphFLA features, closes \(64\%\) of the gap to oracle performance and outperforms the single best solver.

title: HERLMES: Heterogeneous Ensemble with Reinforcement Learning Mechanisms for Evolutionary Search
abstract: This paper proposes HERLMES (Heterogeneous Ensemble with Reinforcement Learning Mechanisms for Evolutionary Search), an ensemble optimization framework that couples evolutionary search with a dimension-aware Q-learning agent using experience replay to adaptively select among five complementary operators. The method introduces a compact 7-dimensional state representation and a novel Success-History Fusion Averaging (SHFA) operator, which extends the Success-History Intelligent Optimizer (SHIO) via time-decaying perturbations and triple-elite averaging. The framework integrates Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), Interior Point Method (IPM), Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP), and SHFA. Experiments on CEC 2017 (30 functions) at \(D\!=\!10,30,50,100\) (51 runs per function) show that HERLMES ranks first by Friedman test across all tested dimensionalities. Ablation studies comprising eight variants confirm the necessity of the ensemble structure, local search components, and dimension-aware reinforcement learning (RL). The source code of HERLMES is publicly available for download at https://github.com/microhard1999/CODES.

title: Island-DR-ALNS: A Diversity-Driven Multi-agent Framework for Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Reinforcement Learning-based Combinatorial Optimization (RLCO) has emerged as a powerful alternative to handcrafted heuristics in CO. Most existing RLCO approaches rely on a monolithic learning agent that is prone to premature convergence and lack of behavioral diversity. To address this, we propose Island-DR-ALNS, a novel framework that integrates Deep Reinforcement Learning with a decentralized island model architecture. Instead of a single agent, the proposed method deploys a population of heterogeneous agents that cooperatively optimize the parameters of the Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS). To increase agents diversity, Negative Correlated Search is incorporated as a regularization mechanism, which explicitly rewards agents for developing distinct search policies. Furthermore, we introduce a socially-aware state representation that enables agents to contextualize their performance relative to others. Extensive experiments on the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem demonstrate that Island-DR-ALNS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The framework also exhibits strong generalization capabilities, enabling effective zero-shot transfer to distinct problems such as TSP and mTSP without retraining.

title: Latent Representation Learning for Visual Reinforcement Learning with a Classifier System
abstract: The well-known XCS Classifier System (XCS) suffers from the curse of dimensionality of Michigan-style Learning Classifier Systems (LCSs) in Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems. This is particularly detrimental for visual RL problems. To address this issue, we combine XCSF (XCS with hyperrectangle conditions and computed linear prediction) with Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Vector-Quantized VAEs as dimensionality reduction methods leading to AEXCSF, a hybrid deep learning–LCS system. We primarily train AEXCSF in a mixed online-offline training scheme, where data is collected and the VAE trained offline before it is combined with XCSF for online RL training. We also introduce an end-to-end solution that collects data using an untrained XCSF, trains the autoencoder on that data, and then trains the XCSF online in visual RL problems using the frozen autoencoder. Furthermore, we train XCSF with naively downscaled images. Our results demonstrate that our AEXCSF as well as XCS learning on downscaled images can learn the targeted visual RL problems. In particular, our VAE-based AEXCSF can provide much smaller state representation while maintaining competitive performance in most targeted environments. This indicates the potential of enhancing the RL capabilities of LCSs when combining them with a trainable dimensionality reduction method, encouraging further research.

title: On the Influence of the Feature Computation Budget on Per-Instance Algorithm Selection for Black-Box Optimization
abstract: Per-instance algorithm selection (PIAS) takes advantage of complementarity between a set of algorithms by deciding which algorithm to run on a given instance. This decision is based on features of the instances, which, in the context of black-box optimization (BBO), require a part of the optimization budget to be computed. This raises two questions: (a) from which fraction of the budget spent on feature computation does PIAS become worth it for BBO, and (b) which fraction of the budget optimizes the tradeoff between feature accuracy and PIAS performance. To this end, we perform a broad study where PIAS with varying sampling budgets for feature computation is compared to the single best algorithm on a broad range of algorithm selection scenarios. These scenarios consist of two portfolio sizes, three problem sets, 4 dimensionalities, and 10 target budgets. We find that PIAS is viable for the majority of tested scenarios, even when as much as a quarter of the total budget is spent on feature computation. The tradeoff for the fraction of the budget spent on feature computation to maximize the benefit of PIAS is highly dependent on the specific AS scenario. Further, on average 20 percent of PIAS loss to the virtual best solver is explained by the budget spent on feature computation, highlighting the importance of properly accounting for the feature budget.

title: Q-Learning-Integrated Real Coded Genetic Algorithms for the Circle Packing Problem
abstract: The Circle Packing Problem (CPP) is a classical NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem that involves arranging circles within a bounded container to maximize packing density. Due to its high computational complexity, CPP is challenging to solve using conventional optimization techniques. In this paper, a Q-learning-integrated Real-Coded Genetic Algorithm (RCGA) framework is proposed to adaptively control crossover and mutation probabilities. To systematically assess the effectiveness of this adaptive strategy, nine classical RCGA variants constructed using three real-coded crossover operators and three mutation operators are considered, along with their Q-learning-integrated RCGA variants, for a total of 18 variants. All variants are evaluated on standard Packomania benchmark instances. Their performance is assessed using best and mean objective values, along with nonparametric statistical analyses based on the Friedman mean ranking and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The experimental results demonstrate that Q-learning-based adaptive parameter control consistently improves convergence behavior and solution quality compared to static-parameter RCGAs. Among all variants, the RCGA employing Q-learning integrated Burr crossover with polynomial mutation (QL-BX-PLYM) achieves better performance across most benchmark instances, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed adaptive evolutionary framework.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Solving Multimodal Functions with CMA-ES
abstract: In this paper, we investigate dynamic meta-parameter control for the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) through deep reinforcement learning (DRL). We formalize the online adaptation of meta-parameters as a Markov decision process (MDP), where each iteration corresponds to one decision step. Based on this formalization, we integrate a controller designed with proximal policy optimization (PPO) into CMA-ES that adapts the learning rate of the mean and the damping parameter of cumulative step-size adaptation (CSA) during the optimization run. Importantly, the controller preserves all known invariance properties of CMA-ES. We train the PPO model only on the Rastrigin function. The learned controller enables CMA-ES with default population size to solve a variety of multimodal functions: on the Rastrigin function, the PPO-CMA-ES is four times faster than IPOP-CMA-ES, and it is also highly competitive on a variety of other multimodal functions, while maintaining reasonable performance on unimodal functions.

title: A Permutation-Based Reformulation for Approximating Weitzman Diversity for Benchmarking in Multi-objective Optimization
abstract: Diversity indicators are important for assessing Pareto front approximations in evolutionary multi-objective optimization. Weitzman diversity is a recursive set-based function defined on pairwise dissimilarities with strong theoretical properties. However, its exponential complexity makes exact computation infeasible for large point sets. In this paper, we reformulate Weitzman diversity as an optimization problem over removal permutations induced by its recursive definition. Then, we study three heuristics adapted from classical permutation strategies for the Traveling Salesman Problem and propose a new set-based method, the Global Max–Min Heuristic (GMM). Experiments on three-objective Pareto front geometries under coverage and uniformity loss show that the proposed methods are generally consistent with Weitzman diversity while remaining computationally tractable. Overall, GMM achieves the highest induced values.

title: Evolutionary Bi-objective Optimization for Safer Student Cycling Routes: Algorithmic Design and Real-World Validation
abstract: Urban route planning for student cyclists involves balancing safety and environmental exposure in complex metropolitan areas. In cities like Mexico City, cyclists face both high levels of air pollution and elevated crime risks as they navigate dense urban environments. This study formulates a bi-objective routing problem designed to minimize crime risk and air pollution exposure using real-world data sources. A large-scale bicycle network has been constructed around a university-centered area, incorporating multiple destinations relevant to student mobility. The proposed framework is evaluated across 30 origin-destination instances, systematically grouped by distance from the starting point, to analyze performance at various spatial scales. As a deterministic baseline, a Multiobjective Dijkstra Algorithm is employed to compute the exact Pareto fronts. To enhance computational scalability, two evolutionary multiobjective approaches based on NSGA-II are introduced. These methods include a novel path-preserving mutation operator that maintains route feasibility while improving exploration of the search space. Experimental results show that the proposed evolutionary approaches provide high-quality approximations of the exact Pareto fronts with significantly lower computational costs, emphasizing their suitability for large-scale, real-world routing applications.

title: From Population to Individual: A New Evolutionary Model for Multi-Objective CMA-ES
abstract: The covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) is a prevailing evolutionary algorithm for single-objective optimisation, in which a population of individuals shares a common probability distribution, aiming to converge rapidly to a single optimal solution. When extended to multi-objective optimisation, CMA-ES (termed as MO-CMA-ES) allows each individual to maintain its own distribution, with the aim of exploring and approaching different regions of the Pareto front. However, in many problems, the reachability of different (promising) regions in the search space can be very different; some regions are easy to reach, while others are more difficult. Standard practice in MO-CMA-ES, which always compare offspring with other solutions in the entire population, may easily discard individuals that have the potential to reach different promising regions but currently are relatively underperformed. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel evolutionary model for MO-CMA-ES that restricts comparison only between offspring and its parent, rather than across the entire population. That is, a newly generated individual is preserved as long as it is better than its parent, regardless of its performance relative to others in the population. In addition, we develop a new restart strategy when the search progress of one individual is detected to stagnate. Experiments on the bi-objective BBOB benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Hybrid Adaptive RL Preference Learning in Multi-objective Portfolio Optimisation
abstract: The Cardinality Constrained Portfolio Optimisation Problem (CCPOP) is an NP-hard challenge in finance, requiring simultaneous minimisation of risk and maximisation of return under strict cardinality and weight constraints. Traditional Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) approximate the entire Pareto front and often struggle to escape local optima in the search space. This paper proposes a framework, Hybrid Adaptive Preference Reinforcement Learning guided by Iterated Local Search, integrated into NSGA-II and driven by synthetic investor profiles via an RL-inspired adaptive selection mechanism. In this mechanism, an embedded agent learns to switch dynamically between diverse user profiles (conservative, neutral, aggressive, risk taker) based on immediate local search improvements. By modelling the local search as a sequential decision process, the agent employs a weighted average estimator to track the value of each preference profile and optimise the search trajectory. Applied to the CCPOP on benchmark datasets, our approach demonstrates that the adaptive mechanism significantly improves convergence and diversity compared to static preference models, offering a robust framework for preference-guided portfolio search.

title: Hybrid Multiobjective Evolutionary Search for Realistic Synthetic Face Image Generation
abstract: This article presents a hybrid multiobjective evolutionary algorithm designed to explore the latent space of a Generative Adversarial Network for the production of realistic synthetic human faces. By integrating a Support Vector Machine to identify critical hyperplanes within the latent search space, the method uses problem-dependent knowledge to guide an adaptive Gaussian operator, ensuring demographic diversity and search efficiency. The optimization process simultaneously targets two conflicting objectives: face similarity to a reference identity and specific race attributes. Evaluated against a benchmarking dataset of diverse ages, genders, and races, the proposed approach demonstrated significant improvements over traditional evolutionary baselines, achieving a relative hypervolume increase between 1.4% and 15.4%. The resulting synthetic images successfully deceived state-of-the-art facial recognition systems, highlighting the usefulness of the method in evaluating and enhancing the robustness of biometric security frameworks.

title: Learning-Augmented Cluster-Wise Prediction for Dynamic Multi-Objective Optimization
abstract: Prediction-based response strategies are widely used in dynamic multi-objective optimization because they exploit historical information to reconstruct the population after environmental changes. However, many existing methods approximate population movement by a single centroid or a global displacement, which implicitly assumes homogeneous evolution across the population. This assumption may become unreliable in complex dynamic environments, where different population regions can move with different magnitudes or even directions. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Learning-Augmented Interval-Similarity-guided Cluster-wise Prediction Strategy (LA-ISCPS), which reformulates post-change response as change-aware subpopulation motion prediction. Specifically, interval similarity is used to estimate change severity and determine the prediction granularity adaptively; a gated recurrent unit (GRU) models historical centroid displacements to predict cluster-wise motion; and an uncertainty-aware Gaussian perturbation mechanism is introduced to compensate for prediction bias and maintain exploration. In our implementation, the generated response population is used to initialize Multi-objective Artificial Physics Optimization Improved by Partition-guided Evolution (PEMOAPO) after each detected environmental change. Experimental results on representative Farina-Deb-Amato (FDA) and dynamic multi-objective optimization problem (DMOP) benchmarks show that the resulting method achieves strong performance across most dynamic settings. Cross-optimizer experiments further indicate that LA-ISCPS is effective beyond a single optimizer, especially when population regions exhibit heterogeneous motion patterns.

title: Multi-objective Approaches for Leakage-Safe Compact Prediction on Temporal Logs
abstract: Temporally ordered interaction logs are promising for predictive modeling, but evaluating search methods on such data is difficult because temporal leakage must be avoided by respecting time-specific availability constraints and deployment may favor compact models. We study leakage-safe compact prediction under a mixed-variable bi-objective formulation in which feature selection and discrete model configuration are optimized jointly. We compare NSGA-II and Random Search under the same candidate space, learning algorithm, evaluation procedure, final solution selection strategy, and matched evaluation budget, thereby separating validation-side search quality from deployment-side robustness. We also include two 40-feature controls, namely a default 40-feature control and a validation-only tuned 40-feature control, to test whether feature selection is needed. The tuned 40-feature control improves validation performance over the default control but remains far below the search-based methods on test, supporting feature selection in this setting. On the validation side, NSGA-II finds stronger compactness–performance trade-offs and uses fewer features, but its selected solutions show a larger validation-to-test transfer gap. Under the final solution selection strategy, this advantage does not translate into statistically supported test-time superiority. These results show that optimizer evaluation on temporally ordered interaction logs under leakage risk must distinguish validation-side search quality from deployment-side robustness.

title: Multitask Pareto Optimization for Monotone Submodular Problems with Dynamic Constraints
abstract: Evolutionary multitasking is a recent approach that solves multiple related optimization problems within a single evolutionary run, rather than addressing each problem separately. We consider monotone submodular optimization problems with dynamic knapsack constraints and study a multitasking formulation in which all tasks share a common monotone submodular function f, but differ in their constraints. We focus on the case where elements within each constraint have uniform cost and show that this structure leads to small Pareto fronts in the multitasking formulation. This enables solution sharing across tasks and can improve performance compared to running standard evolutionary approaches independently, depending on the constraint regime. Using rigorous runtime analysis, we analyze the expected time until the proposed multitasking algorithms obtain a \((1 - 1/e)\)-approximation for each task. Experimental results for the Maximum Coverage problem complement the theoretical analysis and provide further insight into the practical behavior of the approach across different budget settings.

title: Objective-Induced Bias and Search Dynamics in Multiobjective Unsupervised Feature Selection
abstract: Unsupervised feature selection is commonly formulated as a multiobjective optimisation problem that jointly optimises subset quality and subset size. Yet the behaviour of this formulation depends critically on the choice of evaluation objective, the direction of subset-size regularisation, and the initialisation strategy. We study these factors in a controlled setting using a synthetic dataset with known informative, redundant, and irrelevant feature types. Six formulations are compared by combining three evaluation objectives: accuracy, silhouette score, and PCA reconstruction loss with subset-size minimisation or maximisation. The results show that formulation strongly affects both search dynamics and the quality of the resulting Pareto front. Silhouette-based formulations exhibit a strong bias toward trivial low-cardinality solutions and remain weak proxies for predictive performance. In contrast, the proposed PCA loss objective produces compact subsets with test accuracy comparable to subsets obtained by directly optimising supervised accuracy. Overall, the study shows that the design of objective(s) is central to effective multiobjective unsupervised feature selection.

title: Operator-Host Compatibility: When Does IVF Help SPEA2, NSGA-II, or NSGA-III?
abstract: In vitro fertilization (IVF) intensification has been adapted separately to SPEA2, NSGA-II, and NSGA-III. Whether these couplings behave alike under a common protocol has not been tested; we show that they do not. Across 51 synthetic benchmark instances with two and three objectives, IVF/SPEA2 improves its host in most instances, IVF/NSGA-III helps in fewer cases, and IVF/NSGA-II stays close to neutral; endpoint and search-dynamics analyses give the same ordering. IVF benefit therefore depends on the host: it is largest when the host’s selection provides a fine-grained, directionally informative signal.

title: Performance Indicators for Anytime Performance Analysis of Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: The hypervolume (HV) indicator is widely used in evolutionary multi-objective optimization for evaluating the performance of multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). However, in anytime performance analysis, the comparison results based on HV depend strongly on the choice of the reference point. A standard reference point close to the nadir point often results in zero HV values in early generations, making it only weakly Pareto compliant. In contrast, a faraway reference point can produce non-zero HV values at every generation, but it may bias the evaluation toward boundary solutions of the Pareto front. To address these difficulties, this paper proposes a variant of the HV indicator for anytime performance analysis, called \(I_{\textrm{HV}_2}\). The proposed indicator is defined as a weighted sum of two HV values computed using a standard reference point and a faraway reference point. We analyze the approximate optimal distributions of solutions for several representative Pareto front shapes to compare \(I_{\textrm{HV}_2}\) with the standard HV indicator and its existing variant. We also examine the anytime performance of six MOEAs on artificial and real-world multi-objective problems. Experimental results show that \(I_{\textrm{HV}_2}\) can differentiate algorithm performance in early generations while avoiding a clear bias toward either boundary or interior solutions in later generations.

title: A Scalable Benchmark Test Suite for Dynamic Multi-objective Optimization with a Changing Number of Objectives
abstract: Dynamic multi-objective optimization with a changing number of objectives has recently attracted increasing attention due to its relevance to real-world problems whose evaluation criteria may evolve over time. However, existing benchmark test suites for this problem setting suffer from a fundamental limitation: when the number of objectives changes, the objective functions themselves also change implicitly. This makes it difficult to isolate and evaluate an algorithm’s capability to handle dynamics in the number of objectives alone. In this paper, we analyze this issue in detail and show that several theoretical properties claimed in prior studies rely on an assumption that is violated by commonly used test suites. To address this problem, we propose a scalable benchmark test suite in which the objective functions are fixed throughout the optimization process, while the number of active objectives changes over time. Our benchmark is constructed by defining a maximum-objective problem and dynamically selecting subsets of objectives. To avoid degeneracy issues in classical DTLZ and WFG problems, we adopt Minus-DTLZ and Minus-WFG formulations, in which all objectives are mutually conflicting. Extensive benchmark studies using representative algorithms from the literature demonstrate the usefulness and flexibility of the proposed test suite.

title: Pooling with Optimal Hypervolume Subset Selection for Bi-objective Evolutionary Optimization
abstract: The ability to linearly converge to optimal solutions of simple test problems is often regarded desirable in single-objective black-box optimization. It is less commonly studied in multi-objective optimization, and the number of algorithms that have been found capable of linear convergence to optimal solutions is small. We examine whether pooling and optimal hypervolume subset selection can be used to increase rates of linear convergence in bi-objective evolution strategies. Computer experiments on simple test problems suggest that optimal selection from a pool of points can indeed enable solving bi-objective black-box optimization problems with fewer function evaluations compared to algorithms that select sequentially based on individual hypervolume contributions. We then consider a set of more difficult test problems in order to evaluate whether the findings carry weight in a broader context.

title: Population-Aware Contrastive Surrogates for Expensive Multiobjective Optimization
abstract: Expensive multiobjective optimization problems are challenging due to the high cost of objective evaluations. We propose FSMOEA, a foresight-enhanced surrogate-assisted evolutionary framework that improves contrastive surrogate modeling by incorporating population-aware representations. The key idea is to equip surrogate models with a foresight head that embeds solutions into a representation space aligned with the current population, enabling more consistent pairwise comparisons under evolving selection criteria. In addition, FSMOEA performs evolutionary search in a learned low-dimensional space, improving scalability in high-dimensional settings while reducing computational cost. The proposed framework is modular and can be readily integrated into existing classification- and relation-based SMOEAs. We provide theoretical insights into population-dependent surrogate consistency and latent-space optimization. Experiments on 107 benchmarks demonstrate that FSMOEA consistently improves convergence and solution quality over state-of-the-art methods. Source code will be made publicly available.

title: Preference Guided Multiobjective Bayesian Optimization with Aspiration and Reservation Levels
abstract: Multiobjective Bayesian optimization methods address expensive optimization problems involving multiple conflicting objectives. In these methods, acquisition functions, such as expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI), play a key role in determining the next solution to evaluate. When a decision maker, a domain expert, has specific preferences, it is desirable for the acquisition function to guide the search toward solutions of interest, which motivates preference-guided methods. In this paper, we introduce two EHVI-based acquisition functions that incorporate preferences through aspiration and reservation levels, which represent the decision maker’s full satisfaction and dissatisfaction, respectively, with a candidate solution’s objective function values. These modified EHVIs, ARES and EHVI-AR, focus the search on objectives that have not yet reached the specified levels, thereby reducing unnecessary computational cost. ARES favors balanced trade-offs, while EHVI-AR favors better objective function values. We also propose a new performance indicator, ARC-HV, which considers only regions defined by the aspiration and reservation levels. Empirical evaluations show that ARES and EHVI-AR can find solutions that comply with preference information more quickly than a standard multiobjective Bayesian optimization method using EHVI.

title: Revisiting the DMulti-MADS and NSGA-II Algorithms on Novel Benchmarks
abstract: This paper compares Direct Multi-Mesh Adaptive Direct Search (DMulti-MADS) and Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) on real-world and artificial constrained multiobjective optimisation problems. A previous study reported that DMulti-MADS outperformed NSGA-II on simplified versions of biobjective solar power plant problems, as well as other benchmarks. While informative, those experiments favored DMulti-MADS by excluding the original Solar problems and by providing it with starting solutions unavailable to NSGA-II. To address the bias, we conduct a fairer comparison by testing both algorithms on the simplified and original biobjective Solar problems, as well as on the Selected Test Problems (STEP) suite. Each algorithm is evaluated both with and without seeded starting solutions. Results show that DMulti-MADS performs competitively when provided with a good starting solution and limited evaluation budget, whereas NSGA-II exhibits stronger global search abilities and robustness on complex, multimodal problems. This study also contributes a reusable protocol for fairly comparing local derivative-free methods with population-based evolutionary algorithms under matched initialisation and budget assumptions. To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark study to report results on the original biobjective Solar formulations. However, the broader methodological contribution makes the conclusions relevant beyond the Solar suite itself.

title: SPEA2 $$^+$$ : Improved Density Estimation in SPEA2 with Provable Runtime Guarantees
abstract: The Strength Pareto Evolutionary Algorithm 2 (SPEA2) is a popular and prominent evolutionary algorithm for solving multi-objective optimisation problems. Despite its popularity, theoretical analyses of SPEA2 have only appeared recently. Moreover, these analyses focus exclusively on how SPEA2 handles non-dominated solutions and disregard the algorithmic components responsible for handling dominated solutions. We conduct a first runtime analysis of SPEA2 for which these components are analysed. We prove that, unlike other prominent algorithms, including NSGA-II, NSGA-III and SMS-EMOA under the same setting of constant population size and duplicate elimination, SPEA2 is unable to cover the Pareto front of the OneTrapZeroTrap benchmark efficiently. Our results indicate that using k-th nearest-neighbour distance in the fitness assignment provides an insufficient signal to maintain diversity among dominated individuals. To address this issue, we propose an improved variant, SPEA2\(^{+}\), that considers all pairwise distances. The new algorithm achieves the same performance guarantees as the other prominent algorithms on OneTrapZeroTrap, while matching the performance of the original SPEA2 on simpler problems. Experimental results complement our theoretical findings.

title: Toward a Better NSGA-III: Addressing Consistency, Stability, and Uniformity
abstract: NSGA-III is among the most widely used and effective algorithms for many-objective optimization. However, the original NSGA-III does not specify how to resolve the degenerate cases that arise on highly irregular Pareto fronts, so every third-party implementation must introduce its own exception-handling procedures, and these choices can affect performance. Among existing implementations, pymoo’s is the strongest; we show that even it can be made more robust. Prior work identified three issues in pymoo’s NSGA-III: i) inconsistent exception-handling behaviors, ii) unstable objective-space normalization under singular conditions, and iii) insufficient selection pressure toward uniformly distributed solutions. In this work, we propose targeted modifications to pymoo’s NSGA-III that address these issues without changing the fundamental algorithmic framework of the original NSGA-III. Because our proposed algorithm (NSGA-III\(^+\)) preserves the core mechanics of NSGA-III, it maintains excellent performance on problems with regular Pareto fronts while significantly improving robustness on real-world problems. We analyze the algorithmic complexity of each modification and provide theoretical guarantees where appropriate. An ablation study empirically confirms that each modification contributes independently to overall performance. On a suite of box-constrained continuous real-world problems, NSGA-III\(^+\) achieves the best hypervolume on the majority of problems, while introducing negligible overhead relative to the evaluation costs of the objectives. Source code is available at https://github.com/HisaoLabSUSTC/NSGA-IIIPlus.

title: Weight-Instance Early Fusion for Neural Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: In neural multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO), it has become standard practice to introduce extra modules for encoding weight vectors into instance features. This work demonstrates that by simply performing early fusion between the objective weights and the instance features—without any additional modules—comparable or even superior performance can be achieved. We introduce Weight-Instance Early Fusion (WIEF), which directly modulates the input features using the corresponding weight components of each objective, serving as a drop-in replacement for complex weight-encoding structures. Motivated by the intrinsic correlation between weights and instance features, WIEF is simple and can be seamlessly integrated into existing neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) backbones. We use the original NCO backbone to learn these weighted instance features, enabling effective handling of subproblems. Further, we incorporate WIEF into three neural MOCO models to demonstrate its effectiveness and versatility. Experimental results on classic MOCO problems demonstrate that WIEF not only achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods using solely the NCO backbone but also elevates their performance to new SOTA levels.

title: DASOF-HSI: Dual-Stage Adaptive Subset Optimization Framework via Improved Harmony Search for Multimodal Mild Cognitive Impairment Detection
abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) can benefit from multimodal digital assessment, but the resulting feature space and ensemble construction process often contain substantial redundancy. To address this issue, we organize model construction for multimodal MCI detection into two coordinated binary subset optimization stages, one for multimodal feature selection and the other for base-learner selection in stacking. Based on this design, we propose DASOF-HSI, a dual-stage adaptive subset optimization framework built on an improved Harmony Search strategy. In the first stage, a compact subset is selected from electrodermal activity, inter-beat interval signals, and digital cognitive-task features, with the search adaptively regulated by harmony-memory diversity. In the second stage, the optimized feature space is fixed and a compact subset of base learners is selected for stacking, where adaptation is guided by learner quality together with memory diversity. Experiments on a dataset of 1,069 older adults show that DASOF-HSI achieves an accuracy of 0.885, a precision of 0.891, a recall of 0.887, and an F1-score of 0.889, outperforming all compared baselines. Comparisons with alternative subset optimization strategies and ablation analyses further show that the proposed framework improves predictive performance under a controlled evaluation protocol while retaining compact feature and learner subsets.

title: Granular Ball Enhanced Multimodal Ant Colony Optimization for the Multi-Solution Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: The multi-solution traveling salesman problem (MSTSP) focuses on identifying multiple routes for the same instance. Existing multimodal ant colony optimization (ACO) methods remain limited by weak structural cues during initialization and inefficient local refinement in complex discrete search spaces. To address these issues, this paper proposes a granular ball enhanced multimodal ACO framework. In particular, a granular ball guided initialization strategy is designed to construct more coherent initial routes, and a granular ball assisted local search mechanism is introduced to refine competitive solutions by prioritizing critical edge modifications. These components are integrated with the original MACO framework, including multi-pheromone evolution and adaptive niching, to support effective multimodal search. Results on 25 benchmark MSTSP instances show that GB-MACO consistently outperforms MACO and several representative methods.

title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Optimization with Matrix-Based 2-Opt for Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: Matrix-based Ant Colony Optimization (MACO) leverages matrix operations to implement the evolutionary operators in ACO, so that High Performance Computing (HPC) facilities can be used to accelerate the efficiency of ACO in solving Traveling Salesman Problems (TSP). However, existing MACO inherently suffers from low accuracy. To address this limitation, this paper proposes Matrix-based 2-opt (M2-opt) to improve the effectiveness of MACO. Particularly, M2-opt utilizes the matrix operations to implement multiple executions of 2-opt in parallel and then selects the best one to finally execute for the largest improvement. To improve the quality of one route as much as possible, M2-opt is executed continuously until no improvement is obtained. Further, for high efficiency, M2-opt is only executed on a small number of the top best routes constructed by MACO. Subsequently, M2-opt is embedded into MACO to solve TSP with high accuracy. Particularly, beyond Matrix-based Ant System (MAS) and Matrix-based Ant Colony System (MACS), which have been developed by prior studies, this paper further implements the other three classic ACOs, namely Elitist AS (EAS), Rank-based AS (RAS), and Max-Min AS (MMAS), via using matrix operations. As a result, totally five MACOs are developed and cooperate with M2-opt to solve TSP effectively and efficiently. Experiments on 20 TSP instances with the number of cities ranging from nearly 50 to 1300 have demonstrated that M2-opt helps the five MACOs find significantly shorter routes with nearly no serious computational burden under HPC.

title: Accelerating Bilevel Evolutionary Multi-objective Optimization via Offline Parametric Pareto Set Learning
abstract: Bilevel multi-objective optimization problems (BLMOPs) suffer from severe computational redundancy due to the nested nature of lower-level evaluations. To address this, we propose a general plug-in predictive warm-start framework designed to accelerate nested bilevel evolutionary algorithms. By identifying a structural similarity between conditional lower-level optimization and Parametric Multi-Objective Optimization (PMO), we repurpose Parametric Pareto Set Learning (PPSL) to train a neural predictive module offline. For newly generated upper-level candidates, this module provides computationally efficient and highly accurate initial solutions. Crucially, rather than deploying the neural network as a standalone exact solver, these predicted solutions are robustly refined by the host optimizer’s native search mechanisms under a strictly restricted evaluation budget. Comprehensive validations on BLEMO-MLS, BLMFO, and MOBEA-DPL demonstrate that the proposed module significantly reduces expensive lower-level function evaluations and computation time.

title: Undersampled MRI Reconstruction with Swarm Intelligence
abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) reconstruction from undersampled k-space remains an ill-posed inverse problem, commonly addressed through Fourier-based techniques, regularised optimisation, and data-driven deep learning methods. This study investigates a derivative-free reconstruction approach based on swarm intelligence, focusing on Dispersive Flies Optimisation (DFO) alongside Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO). The proposed framework formulates MRI reconstruction as a frequency-domain optimisation problem, directly minimising masked k-space discrepancy across coils. Experiments are conducted using synthetic multi-coil phantoms under controlled undersampling. Results indicate that, under the tested settings, tuned DFO achieves comparable reconstruction quality to tuned Sensitivity Encoding (SENSE) and Compressed Sensing (CS) baselines in terms of SSIM and PSNR. The findings also highlight a trade-off between reconstruction quality and computational cost, as well as challenges related to multi-coil behaviour and metric alignment. Overall, the study demonstrates the feasibility of swarm-based optimisation for undersampled MRI reconstruction within a controlled setting, and provides a basis for further investigation into statistical robustness, noise sensitivity, and hybrid optimisation strategies.

title: An Easy-to-Use Extension of Surrogate-Assisted Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms for Expensive Robust Optimization
abstract: Many engineering problems involve expensive-to-evaluate objectives, for which surrogate-assisted multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (SAMOEAs) are highly effective. In practice, however, robust optimal solutions that are insensitive to perturbations in decision variables are often required, while most existing SAMOEAs are not designed for such expensive robust optimization (RO). Rather than developing RO-specific algorithms, a generic extension applicable to a wide range of existing SAMOEAs is highly desirable, as it preserves the advantages of mature algorithmic designs. This paper demonstrates that vanilla SAMOEAs can be easily extended for expensive RO under a severely limited budget of function evaluations. Specifically, we modify a given SAMOEA framework to compute and optimize an estimated robustness metric, the mean effective objective function, by averaging objective values of perturbed samples predicted by surrogate models. We also introduce new challenging multi-objective RO benchmark problems, which are available online. Experimental results show that, without explicit robustness evaluations based on expensive evaluations, the proposed extension enables existing SAMOEAs to effectively search for robust solutions.

title: An Empirical Study on the Realism Gap of Benchmarks for Multi-Objective Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Multi-objective Neural Architecture Search (MO-NAS) simultaneously optimises multiple conflicting objectives such as accuracy, model size, and inference time. Since evaluating candidate architectures is computationally expensive, cheaper proxies, such as tabular, surrogates or mathematical test functions, are used to characterise the performance of MO-NAS algorithms, each compromising on the realism of actual scenarios in different ways.Whether this realism gap affects conclusions drawn from benchmarking MO-NAS methods has received little attention.This paper systematically characterises three types of NAS benchmarks. We empirically show that tabular benchmarks are poor discriminators, often failing to distinguish between methods that behave very differently at realistic scales of the search space. The empirical experiment includes three benchmark types and six architecture-agnostic methods, including a newly proposed framework called SAMOS, that exploits the varying costs of objectives. From the results, we derive actionable recommendations for benchmark selection in future MO-NAS evaluations.

title: Benchmarking the Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms for Solving Non-linear Multi-objective Fixed-Charge Transportation Problems
abstract: In this paper, we study a non-linear multi-objective optimization fixed-cost transportation problem (MO-FCTP) with multiple modes of transport, having two conflicting objectives: minimization of the total transportation cost, respectively distribution time. We developed four novel multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) based on SPEA2 and MOEA/D achieved by using two different representations: priority-based representation, respectively Prüfer-based encoding, and performed a comparison analysis of all the existing MOEAs from the literature.The achieved computational results for a set of benchmark instances show that our proposed MOEAs are competitive against the current state-of-the-art algorithms for solving the considered non-linear MO-FCTP. We also compare the performance of the MOEAs based on the following quality measures: the cardinality of the Pareto fronts, hypervolume and inverted generational distance.

title: Effects of Objective Normalization on Regions of Interest in Preference-Based Evolutionary Multi-objective Optimization
abstract: Preference-based evolutionary multi-objective optimization (PBEMO) aims to approximate a region of interest (ROI) defined by the preference information from a decision maker (DM). Although objective functions in real-world applications typically have different scales, the issue of how to define the ROI in such problems has been overlooked in the literature. In fact, it has not been standardized in the EMO community whether the ROI should be defined in the unnormalized objective space or in the normalized objective space. In this context, this paper investigates the effects of objective normalization on ROIs. First, this paper shows that two ROIs defined in the unnormalized and normalized objective spaces can differ significantly for problems with differently scaled objectives. Then, we demonstrate that ROIs defined in the normalized objective space are highly difficult to approximate even on problems with equally scaled objectives because of poor approximations of the ideal and nadir points. In contrast, we show that ROIs defined in the unnormalized objective space are much easier to approximate than those defined in the normalized objective space.

title: Efficient Multi-child Recombination for Bi-objective NK Landscapes: A Comparison to Exact Pareto Fronts
abstract: Benchmarking multi-objective optimization algorithms for pseudo-Boolean functions is difficult due to the lack of test problems with known exact Pareto fronts, particularly for large problems. This paper introduces three contributions. First, we develop a new dynamic programming paradigm that can find the exact Pareto front for bi-objective Boolean problems with bounded tree-width and bounded integer outputs. Second, we introduce test problems for bi-objective adjacent NK landscapes where the exact optimal Pareto front solution is known. Third, we introduce a new multi-child version of Partition Crossover that can yield multiple children from one crossover event. We use this multi-child crossover operator in combination with the multi-objective DRILS (Deterministic Recombination and Iterated Local Search) algorithm, DRILS-MO, designed for Boolean and pseudo-Boolean optimization problems. The new algorithm, McDRILS-MO, makes use of Partition Crossover so that one crossover event can generate multiple children which that can be used to populate the best-so-far Pareto Front with multiple non-dominated solutions with minimal additional computation cost. Experiments with up to N = 100,000 variables shows McDRILS-MO achieves dense Pareto front coverage and near-optimal hypervolume at very low cost comparable to other methods.

title: Evolutionary Algorithms and Multi-objective Minimum Spanning Trees with Limited Distinct Weight Values
abstract: Evolutionary algorithms have been used for a wide range of multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Despite practical success, theoretical results on the runtime of evolutionary algorithms for multi-objective combinatorial problems are rather limited. One classical problem that has been investigated is the multi-objective minimum spanning tree problem for which runtime bounds have been obtained to compute all extremal corner points of the Pareto front. With this paper, we provide some more detailed insights into the structure of the Pareto front when the edge weights take on a small number of distinct values. Based on these insights, we derive new runtime results for evolutionary multi-objective algorithms and complement our theoretical results with experimental investigations.

title: A Superlinearly Convergent Evolution Strategy
abstract: We present a hybrid algorithm between an evolution strategy and a quasi Newton method. The design is based on the Hessian Estimation Evolution Strategy, which iteratively estimates the inverse square root of the Hessian matrix of the problem. This is akin to a quasi-Newton method and corresponding derivative-free trust-region algorithms like NEWUOA. The proposed method therefore replaces the global recombination step commonly found in non-elitist evolution strategies with a quasi-Newton step. Numerical results show superlinear convergence, resulting in improved performance in particular on smooth convex problems.

title: Accelerating Multi-objective Bayesian Optimisation via Predictive-Gradient Catalysts
abstract: This paper presents a general acceleration mechanism for multi-objective Bayesian optimisation (MOBO) that leverages Gaussian process predictive gradients as auxiliary signals. Rather than replacing existing Pareto-compliant acquisition functions, the proposed approach augments them with local stationarity information derived from surrogate-derived gradients, enabling faster convergence toward the global Pareto set under limited evaluation budgets. Two catalyst instantiations are investigated: an adaptive Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm-Based Catalyst (MGDA) and a predefined-weight variant that enables focused exploration when budgets are tight. Experiments on the DTLZ benchmark suite (using 2 objectives and 10 decision variables) show that predictive gradient catalysis can deliver significant acceleration compared to other acquisition functions (EHVI, AugTch, tMPoI, SAF) when surrogates are accurate, particularly for stationary problems. title: Feature and Similarity-Based Explainability of Experimental Materials Data via Black-Box Hyperparameter Optimization
abstract: Building automated pipelines for scientific interpretation of experimental data remains a challenge. We propose a two-stage automated analysis pipeline in which both model-selection steps are formulated as black-box optimization problems over mixed, non-convex hyperparameter spaces and solved with Tree-structured Parzen Estimation (TPE). The first stage explains an automatically tuned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) regressor with SHAP and permutation feature importance. The second stage extends this parameter-level explainability with cognitively motivated object-level similarity estimation. It extracts stimulus-free similarities from the representations of an automatically tuned classifier trained on functional responses. This extends the approach from the large vision networks domain to small MLPs trained on scarce experimental tabular data. Evaluated on a new solid-foam dataset for pressure-drop and heat-transfer prediction, the pipeline recovers physically meaningful feature attributions and achieves superior or comparable results to a stimulus-based similarity baseline under a physics-informed, overlap-based evaluation.

title: Few-Shot Constrained Bayesian Optimization for Dynamic Constrained Problem
abstract: Many real-world optimization problems are non-stationary, where both objective functions and constraints evolve over time due to changing environments. Existing Constrained Bayesian Optimization (CBO) methods are primarily designed for static landscapes and fail to adapt to such temporal shifts. This paper introduces DCBO, a CBO framework for dynamic problems under limited evaluation budgets, which leverages historical information to track evolving constraint boundaries while balancing exploitation within the feasible region. We introduce an ensemble model that aggregates historical models from previous time steps to predict the objective and constraint functions at the next time step. To navigate the search space, we propose an adaptive acquisition function that dynamically balances exploitation within the feasible region and exploration along the constraint boundary. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on synthetic benchmarks and real-world applications across various domains demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method. The source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DCBO-D0FC/README.md.

title: Policy-Targeted Evolutionary Entropy Search for Zero-Shot Contextual Optimization
abstract: The expensive contextual optimization problem (ECOP) involves optimizing black-box functions that depend on design variables and context variables under limited evaluation budget. In many real-time applications, zero-shot generalization is crucial, where the objective is to learn a policy mapping contexts to high-quality solutions that generalizes effectively to unseen contexts without requiring additional evaluations during deployment. The challenge lies in efficiently exploring the joint context-solution space to acquire informative observations that improve the policy’s generalization. We propose policy-targeted evolutionary entropy search (PTEES), an approach that selects evaluation points to maximize information gain about the holistic policy mapping. To enable sample-efficient acquisition, PTEES constructs a discrete approximation of the joint context-solution space through representative context sampling and support set pre-screening, reducing computational complexity while preserving task correlations. Policy-space entropy is approximated by incrementally updating the Gaussian process posterior with fantasy observations corresponding to sampled policy instances. Furthermore, PTEES maintains and evolves a non-parametric search distribution over the joint space, combining historical promising regions with newly discovered high-value candidates. This evolutionary distribution learning mechanism naturally propagates knowledge across contexts while balancing exploration and exploitation. Experiments on ECOP benchmark demonstrate that PTEES achieves superior zero-shot generalization performance across unseen contexts compared to state-of-the-art contextual Bayesian optimization methods.

title: Scaling Bayesian Optimization to High-Dimension via Pairwise-Relation-Based Decomposition
abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely utilized for solving expensive black-box optimization problems in various domains. However, BO is limited by the curse of dimensionality. Recent research has shown that extending BO with dimension-level decomposition can yield both theoretical and practical improvements, but how to obtain effective decomposition remains as an open challenge. In this work, we point out that the prevailing full-dimension likelihood-based decomposition methods can hardly identify the structural information among dimensions. Instead, we propose a simple yet effective Pairwise-Relation-Based Decomposition (PRBD) framework, which utilizes metrics to quantify the pairwise interaction of dimensions, and groups them by clustering. Specifically, we design three metrics from different perspectives to quantify the pairwise relation of dimensions, including average goodness, pairwise marginal likelihood, and polynomial regression. Due to the scarce data under the settings of BO, PRBD can be more reliable than the decomposition based on full-dimension likelihood. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world problems demonstrate that PRBD consistently obtains effective decompositions and achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art BO methods on high-dimensional problems.

title: Surrogate Prediction of Evolutionary Algorithm Tournaments for Traffic Model Calibration
abstract: Surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithms (SAEAs) are commonly used to reduce the cost of optimisation when objective function evaluations are expensive, such as in traffic model calibration. Traditional approaches approximate the objective function using regression models or rank the full population. However, many evolutionary algorithms rely on tournament selection, which only requires relative comparisons between a few candidate solutions rather than accurate fitness estimates or full population ranking. This observation motivates an alternative surrogate approach based on pairwise ranking. Tournament selection can be decomposed into binary comparisons of the form: is one solution fitter than another? This enables the use of surrogate models that directly predict tournament outcomes. In this work, we propose tournament prediction surrogates, both classification and regression forms, and compare with standard fitness approximation surrogates. Experiments on three continuous benchmark problems and a real-world traffic calibration problem with 1,574 parameters demonstrate tournament-based surrogates offer advantages in high-dimensional settings.

title: A Parallel $$\epsilon $$ -Constraint Quantum Optimizer for Bi-objective Pseudo-Boolean Problems
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QA-OA) is a well-established quantum method for combinatorial optimization, originally designed for single-objective problems. Existing multi-objective QAOA extensions typically rely on decomposition approaches; mainly weighted-sum aggregation. The former has shortfalls when dealing with some types of Pareto fronts (e.g., non-convex ones), which restricts the applicability of the multi-objective QAOA. On the other hand, today’s quantum machines are in their Noisy Intermediate-Scale era (NISQ), which hardens even more any practical application. In this perspective, this work attempts to advance multi-objective quantum optimization by devising (I) a parallel quantum multi-objective QAOA that explores the potential of \(\varepsilon \)-constraint methods, (II) by analyzing their main design aspects in the quantum realm, including (III) grid and iterative threshold selection, (IV) exact and approximated constraint handling, as well as (V) their classical and quantum handling. The proposed method is evaluated using diverse bi-objective benchmarks of 10–20 variables, with an increasing size, and features, and compared with state-of-the-art multi-objective QAOA as well as classical optimizers. The results demonstrate that the \(\varepsilon \)-constraint-based proposal is a promising and NISQ-suited alternative for bi-objective optimization under extreme configurations.

title: Circuit-Aware Hyperparameter Prediction for MPS Quantum Simulators
abstract: Matrix Product State (MPS) methods are among the most effective approaches for the classical simulation of large-scale quantum circuits, but their practical efficiency depends strongly on hyperparameter settings. These settings can substantially affect both run time and fidelity, and the performance achieved by a given configuration may vary considerably from one circuit to another. Finding suitable settings is itself expensive, since each candidate configuration must be evaluated through circuit simulation. To enable fast circuit-specific MPS hyperparameter selection, we propose a two-stage optimization-plus-learning framework. In the first stage, we perform costly offline single-objective CMA-ES optimization under a fidelity constraint and build a training database. In the second stage, we define circuit features that capture MPS-relevant structural properties and train a circuit-aware hybrid ranking model to rapidly recommend MPS hyperparameter configurations for unseen circuits without additional simulations. We evaluate the approach on multiple scalable circuit families using leave-one-family-out and size-based validation. The results show that offline optimization often improves over default settings, although the magnitude of the gain depends strongly on the backend, circuit family, and circuit scale. The predictor recovers a meaningful fraction of this improvement, performs better under size-based validation than under family-based transfer, and generally remains below the offline optimum.

title: Evolutionary Design of Parameterized Quantum Circuits for Classification and Reinforcement Learning Tasks
abstract: This paper extends Evolutionary eXploration of Augmenting Quantum Circuits (EXAQC), a unified framework for the automated design and optimization of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) to include reinforcement learning tasks. Designing effective quantum circuits is challenging as the performance of a circuit is highly dependent on architecture, including gate composition, qubit interactions, and depth, as well as the target quantum system. Traditional approaches relying on fixed templates or heuristic designs often fail to generalize across tasks. To address this, EXAQC formulates circuit construction as a distributed evolutionary optimization problem, jointly exploring circuit structure and parameters in parallel worker processes using mutation and crossover operators. Experiments on 4 standard classification benchmarks demonstrate that EXAQC achieves competitive or superior accuracy with more efficient circuits. Additionally, evaluations on 4 different reinforcement learning environments show that evolved circuits can learn effective policies and reach near-optimal rewards with relatively low parameter counts. Overall, EXAQC provides a scalable, task-adaptive approach for quantum circuit discovery, highlighting the potential of evolutionary methods in advancing quantum machine learning.

title: Generation of Optimised Quantum Oracles Using Grammar-Based Genetic Programming
abstract: Quantum search algorithms, most notably Grover’s algorithm, offer a significant quadratic speedup over their classical counterparts. The practical realisation of this advantage, however, depends critically on the efficient implementation of a quantum oracle. This oracle functions as a problem-specific “black box”, essential for identifying the desired solutions within the quantum state space. This work tackles the challenge of optimising oracle circuits using grammar-based genetic programming. The objective is to automatically generate circuits that optimise for depth and exhibit greater composability than solutions currently found in the literature. To this end, an abstract grammar was developed to ensure the generation of valid oracles. This grammar is integrated into a genetic programming algorithm that generates circuits. To ensure the validity of each solution, a repair mechanism is applied, and each solution is optimised by a mechanism that removes redundant gates. The evaluation process is based on computing the depth of the generated circuit. The experiments conducted show that the proposed algorithm produces oracles with lower depth than other automatic methods reported in the literature. Oracles were evaluated for conditions such as “less than”, “greater than”, “multiples of”, and “prime numbers”, as well as for complex combinations among them. The results suggest that grammar-based genetic programming is an effective technique for automating the synthesis of valid and efficient quantum oracles.

title: Analysis of the Effect of Multiplicative Noise on the $$(\mu / \mu _w, \lambda )$$ -ES Under Two Noise Models
abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) are effective optimizers in noisy settings, where their selection mechanism provides an inherent strength against uncertainty in the objective function. In the setting of multiplicative noise, this paper analyzes the impact of two different noise formulations on the selection mechanism of the \((\mu / \mu _w, \lambda )\)-ES. In particular, we compare a log-normal noise model with its first-order approximation and show that their selection dynamics differ in the limit of large noise strength. Using a step-size proportional to the distance to the optimum, we relate the expected logarithmic progress to almost sure linear convergence and analyze the resulting convergence rates. Although the models differ in finite dimensions, we show that their asymptotic convergence rates coincide as the dimension tends to infinity.

title: QuantumGS: Quantum Encoding Framework for Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Recent advances in neural rendering, particularly 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have framed scene reconstruction as a complex iterative optimization problem. However, standard 3DGS relies on classical spherical harmonics, which often struggle to accurately converge on high-frequency, view-dependent effects such as sharp reflections and transparency. While hybrid approaches mitigate this using classical Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), they remain limited by the expressivity of classical networks in low-parameter regimes. In this paper, we bridge the gap between natural computing and rendering by introducing QuantumGS, a novel hybrid framework that integrates Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC), computational models derived from quantum mechanics, into the iterative optimization pipeline of 3DGS. We propose a dedicated unique encoding strategy that maps viewing directions directly onto the Bloch sphere, exploiting the intrinsic geometry of qubit state space to represent three dimensional directional information. Furthermore, we replace classical color modulation networks with quantum circuits instantiated via a hypernetwork or conditioning mechanism. This design increases representational expressivity and improves generalization across the optimization landscape. Source code is available at https://github.com/gwilczynski95/QuantumGS.

title: Tightening the Calculation Gap in Quantum Multi-objective Pseudo-Boolean Optimisation
abstract: Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) is a quantum combinatorial optimiser designed for Single-Objective (SO) problems, and recently extended to Multi-Objective (MO) ones. Its efficiency depends on the parameterisation of its quantum circuit, which requires an iterative interaction between a quantum machine and a classical one. It guarantees solution optimality under extreme-regime configurations, but its quantum-classical interaction overhead is a bottleneck towards practical use even under moderate-efficiency requirements, especially considering today’s costly, noisy, and limited quantum machines. This work attempts to bring the MO-QAOA’s execution to a practical-use scale in low-efficiency regimes, and also quantum advantage in the higher ones. This is done by devising and exploring a Machine Learning (ML)-assisted MO-QAOA that is (I) scalable through parallelisation, (II) extendable to different problems and scalarisations, assisted by (III) generalisable non/neural models, (VI) based on architecture search using an evolutionary linkage-learning algorithm, that (V) considers three feature modelings capturing the problem/circuit properties. (VI) The experiments were conducted on the largest settings in the MO-QAOA literature so far, including problems of 1–5 objectives, 9–156 variables, using 2–11 parallel workers running 9/31-qubit quantum simulators and 4 of the 133/156-qubit largest gate-based quantum machines worldwide. Comparison shows that the ML-assisted MO-QAOA is competitive to the standard MO-QAOA in some cases, and more efficient/faster in others.

title: Developing a Novel Comorbidities Index for Predicting 10-Year Mortality in Prostate Cancer Patients: A Computational Data-Driven Approach
abstract: The Charlson Comorbidities Index (CCI) is a weighted additive index widely used to estimate ten-year mortality risk, but its original weights may not reflect contemporary prognoses. This limitation is critical in Prostate Cancer (PCa), where radical treatment is recommended only for patients with a life expectancy of at least ten years. For candidates eligible for Radical Prostatectomy (RP), accurate estimation of ten-year other-cause mortality is essential to balance oncological benefit against competing risks and avoid overtreatment. We propose a data-driven framework to derive a comorbidity index tailored to PCa patients considered for RP. Using a retrospective single-institution cohort, we apply Population Based Bio-Inspired Algorithm (PBBIAs) to recalibrate comorbidity weights and evolve alternative symbolic formulations optimized for ten-year survival discrimination. We compared six optimization strategies, including symbolic regression approaches based on Genetic Programming (GP), population-based metaheuristics, clinically validated baselines, and survival prediction models. Results show that GA, FST-PSO, and SLIM outperform both the original CCI and the Prostate Cancer specific Comorbidity Index (PCCI), particularly when PCa-specific variables are included, improving the Concordance Index by up to 0.1. GPLearn yields compact and interpretable models with competitive performance. Overall, the proposed approach provides an updated and interpretable tool to improve patient selection for RP.
