title: EPL: Evolutionary Prototype Learning for Imbalanced Text Classification
abstract: Class imbalance remains a persistent challenge in text classification, where minority classes are often misclassified due to insufficient training examples. This paper introduces EPL (Evolutionary Prototype Learning), a bio-inspired framework that integrates evolutionary computation with prototype-based learning to address this problem. EPL maintains a population of class prototypes that evolve through elimination, elite selection, and crossover operations, while adaptively expanding to capture intra-class semantic diversity. A reliability-aware weighted prediction mechanism leverages prototype update frequency to improve inference robustness. Experiments on six benchmark datasets under varying imbalance ratios demonstrate that EPL significantly outperforms representative imbalanced classification methods. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each evolutionary component, with the proposed approach maintaining stable performance as imbalance severity increases. The results validate that evolutionary prototype optimization provides an effective solution for imbalanced text classification.

title: ESTI: Evolutionary Signal and Time-Series Inspection for Auditing ECG Classifiers
abstract: Deep learning has markedly improved automatic electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, but strong predictive performance does not reveal what evidence a trained classifier treats as sufficient for each diagnosis. We introduce ESTI (Evolutionary Signal and Time-Series Inspection), a model-agnostic framework for globally auditing frozen multi-label ECG classifiers through evolutionary search in a compact, interpretable procedural signal space. Instead of optimizing raw waveforms, ESTI evolves normalized genomes that control meaningful aspects of synthetic 12-lead ECG generation, including beat morphology, rhythm dynamics, lead-dependent structure, and nuisance components. This formulation supports black-box optimization while preserving interpretability at the level of signal-generation factors. Across all abnormalities, the search successfully elicits strong target responses, but these often co-occur with substantial non-target activation, suggesting that the classifier’s decision space is only partially separated. Evolutionary trajectories further show that several class associations arise early and persist throughout optimization, while parameter-drift analyses reveal that some abnormalities depend on focused procedural directions whereas others rely on broader, less isolated regions of the search space. These results position ESTI as a practical method for auditing the internal evidence structure of ECG classifiers, being easily adapted to other signal and time-series classifiers.

title: E-UPA: Evolutionary Universal Patch Attack via Genetic Programming for Black-Box Scenarios
abstract: Adversarial examples are carefully crafted inputs designed to deceive neural networks by introducing imperceptible perturbations to the original data. Despite advancements in deep learning, even state-of-the-art Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) remain vulnerable to such attacks. While both white-box and black-box adversarial attacks have been extensively studied, the use of evolutionary computation to generate Universal Adversarial Perturbations (UAPs) in black-box scenarios is a growing area of research with significant potential. This work advances this research direction by proposing a novel black-box universal adversarial patch attack, called Evolutionary Universal Patch Attack (E-UPA), which uses a Genetic Programming (GP) approach to generate and optimise adversarial patches. The proposed method evolves image patches that, when applied to images, effectively perturb the target model’s predictions. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 dataset using VGG16 and ResNet50 models demonstrate that the E-UPA achieves high Attack Success Rates (ASR), with values reaching up to 90.39% for ResNet50 and 68.48% for VGG16 under a perturbation threshold of 5% (\(L_{\infty }\)). Furthermore, the attack exhibits strong transferability, particularly for adversarial examples generated for VGG16, which transfer well to other architectures like ResNet101 and VGG19. The proposed method has also been shown to be more efficient and effective compared to existing universal black-box attacks, requiring fewer queries to achieve higher success rates.

title: Evolve While You Train: Online Data Augmentation for Medical Imaging
abstract: Effective deep learning in medical imaging is frequently limited by the lack of large-scale, annotated datasets. While automated data augmentation can improve model generalisation, existing methods often require separate search phases or static policies that are not optimised during training. This paper introduces Data Augmentation Optimiser (DAOP) Online, an evolutionary framework that evolves and optimises data augmentation policies during online model training. By integrating the search process into the training loop, we remove the need for an expensive offline exploration stage. The system employs evolutionary strategies with a snapshot-and-restore mechanism to explore a discrete set of augmentation functions. When combined with continuous probability and magnitude parameters, this creates an effectively infinite search space, all while maintaining the stability of the model weights. The framework was evaluated on the MedMNIST v2 benchmark across various imaging modalities. The results show that DAOP Online consistently identifies modality-specific policies that outperform official baselines and established AutoML methods. We achieved statistically significant improvements in Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) (\(p < 0.05\)), reaching 0.923 for DermaMNIST and 0.956 for PneumoniaMNIST. Furthermore, compared to a projected multi-stage offline evolutionary search, the framework delivers up to a 71% reduction in total GPU-hours. These findings demonstrate that online co-evolution is a practical and efficient solution for automated regularisation in model training.

title: Evolving the Active Set: A Nature-Inspired Pruning Strategy for Budgeted Online Machines
abstract: Online kernel learning algorithms process data streams on the fly and have demonstrated predictive performance. However, their deployment on memory-constrained devices is hindered because the active set of support vectors grows linearly over time. To enforce a hard upper bound on memory usage, budgeted algorithms limit the active set to a fixed size of B instances. Existing budget maintenance mechanisms typically rely on simple, deterministic heuristics—such as randomly discarding instances or deleting those with minimal weights. While efficient, these localized strategies often suffer from myopic information loss, leading to sub-optimal mistake bounds. In this paper, we bridge online kernel learning with evolutionary computation by proposing a nature-inspired pruning strategy. We treat the active set as a biological population with a strict carrying capacity B. When the memory limit is triggered, instead of heuristic deletion, we employ a lightweight evolutionary selection mechanism to evaluate and evolve the subset of instances. By optimizing a fitness function that measures the global predictive contribution and structural information of the candidates, the algorithm dynamically identifies the “fittest” support vectors to survive. To further mitigate information loss, the “eliminated” instances are mathematically projected onto the surviving population. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate that our evolutionary active set outperforms state-of-the-art deterministic budgeted algorithms under the same memory constraints.

title: Large-Scale Testing Global Optimization Methods with Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
abstract: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are of a moderate size and are based on a small number of analytical functions that date back even to 1970’s. This causes a risk of biasing the development of global optimization methods. We argue that the tasks related to the black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) can serve as an element of valuable global optimization benchmark in many-dimensional space. We demonstrate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics in solving example BBAA problems. Thus we take a step towards convergence of global optimization methods to the realistic challenges and needs that arise in the modern machine learning field.

title: Modularity-Based Linkage Model Assisted Gradient Descent for Neural Network Training
abstract: We present Modularity-based Linkage Model Assisted Gradient Descent (MAGD), which trains feedforward neural networks by alternating short AdamW fine-tunes on a population with a gene-pool optimal-mixing step whose crossover masks are learned online. Each generation aligns a parent and a donor with Git Re-Basin, builds a neuron-level proximity graph from their weight magnitudes, and partitions it with the Leiden community detection algorithm to form a Family of Subsets whose elements serve as crossover masks. AdamW first- and second-moment buffers and a per-individual adaptive learning rate persist across generations, so each network accumulates optimiser context despite recombination. Experiments on the 3-bit MNIST-parity MAGD outperforms an ablation without alignment, a single-model AdamW baseline and a population EA without recombination. A code repository is provided at https://github.com/qyk130/MAGD.

title: FastSNO: A Fast Space Net Optimization for Single-Objective Bound Constrained Problems
abstract: The space net optimization (SNO) is a promising metaheuristic algorithm that uses the space net to provide a rough depiction of the landscape of the solution space based on the information of previously searched solutions to improve the search accuracy. Although SNO is capable of using this additional information of the solution space to guide searches, its moderate convergence speed makes it insufficient when the number of evaluations is limited. That is why an improved version of SNO will be presented in this study, which adds (1) an integrated solution generation operator and (2) an adaptive search strategy switch operator for different solution generation mechanisms. With these modifications, we present an accelerated version of SNO to achieve satisfactory results under limited resources. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art metaheuristic algorithms for the CEC2024 and CEC2025 benchmarks in terms of the U-score metrics. The results further show that the SNO-based algorithm can efficiently solve single-objective bound-constrained problems under limited computational resources.

title: Optimizing Transductive Few Shot Learning with Evolutionary Computation
abstract: Few shot learning attempts to scale a classification model (typically in the form of a backbone neural network) to thousands of classes under the constraint of each epoch consisting of a sample of K instances (per class) and M classes (where \(K \in \{1, 5\}, M \in \{20, 5\}\)). We demonstrate that we can: (1) Augment the prototypical approach to few shot learning with an stochastic search for discovering masks that encourage sparse weight distributions. (2) Optimize performance further using an evolutionary transductive boosting approach given an embedding defined by the backbone network. Particular attention is placed on the formulation of the loss function and a balanced Hungarian assignment for the query predictions. Benchmarking on the Omiglot and OmnImage datasets demonstrates that the complexity of the backbone can be reduced by \(\approx \) 60% and 98% respectively without negatively impacting on the classification accuracy.

title: Constrained Hybrid Metaheuristic Algorithm Enhanced with Population Mixing Mechanism
abstract: Combining population-based metaheuristics into hybrid frameworks can improve their performance, especially in black-box continuous optimization. The constrained Hybrid Metaheuristic (cHM) is a recently proposed approach whose key advantage is simplicity: it alternates between a probing phase, where several metaheuristics run independently, and a fit phase, where the best-performing one continues on its population. However, at the end of the probing phase, cHM retains only the population of the best metaheuristic and discards all others, losing potentially valuable information. We address this limitation by proposing several strategies for mixing populations after each probing phase. Drawing inspiration from migration mechanisms in island-based evolutionary algorithms, our strategies offer different approaches to balance fitness and diversity in the combined population. Experiments on BBOB benchmark functions show that cHM with population mixing (cHMpm) clearly outperforms cHM even with simple mixing strategies. We further compare cHMpm with island-based algorithms and demonstrate its competitive results despite being considerably simpler.

title: Deep Tournament Selection for Genetic Algorithms
abstract: In Genetic Algorithms (GAs), the selection operator plays a critical role in balancing exploration and exploitation. However, classical and adaptive selection mechanisms largely rely on static rules or handcrafted heuristics that fail to adapt to the real-time dynamics of the evolving population. In this work, we introduce Deep Tournament Selection (DTS), a novel domain-independent selection operator that reformulates tournament selection as a Markov Decision Process optimized via reinforcement learning. DTS evaluates candidate solutions in a tournament using a Transformer encoder augmented with global and local rank-based positional encodings, along with a self-attention pointer mechanism. This architecture allows the selection policy to jointly capture global fitness relationships and local competitive context. The policy is trained fully online using policy-gradient reinforcement learning without requiring additional fitness evaluations, enabling the operator to dynamically adjust its selection pressure. We evaluate DTS on three canonical combinatorial optimization domains: Graph Coloring, Set Cover, and the Traveling Salesman Problem. Empirical results demonstrate that DTS achieves faster convergence, improved solution quality, and robust performance across problem instances compared to classical and dynamic selection baselines, while introducing negligible computational overhead and preserving population diversity.

title: Individual-Level Parallelism of Genetic Algorithm
abstract: Due to the heterogeneity of genetic strategies among individuals, existing parallel genetic algorithm frameworks typically achieve parallelization through subpopulation partitioning or thread assignment for different individuals. However, these methods mainly parallelize the execution of individuals, while heterogeneous control flows and genetic operation logic still exist across different individuals. As the population size and problem scale increase, thread scheduling and warp divergence introduce additional overhead, leading to increasing computational costs. To address this issue, we propose a tensorized genetic algorithm framework (Tensor-GA), which unifies population representation and genetic operators into a tensor formulation. By leveraging mask-driven tensor operations, heterogeneous evolutionary processes are transformed into a unified computation graph, enabling efficient individual-level parallelism. Building on this, we further introduce EC-AdaGA, an adaptive mechanism based on elite consensus information to enhance global search and escape local optima. Experimental results show that the runtime of Tensor-GA scales sub-linearly with population size, and its computational cost increases significantly more slowly than those of traditional methods and existing parallel frameworks as the problem size grows. EC-AdaGA demonstrates significantly better optimization performance than traditional methods on TSPLIB benchmarks.

title: Multi-task Optimization over Networks of Tasks
abstract: Multi-task optimization is a powerful approach for solving a large number of tasks in parallel. However, existing algorithms face distinct limitations: Population-based methods scale poorly and remain underexplored for large task sets. Approaches that do scale beyond a thousand tasks are mostly MAP-Elites variants and rely on a fixed, discretized archive that disregards the topology of the task space. We introduce MONET (Multi-Task Optimization over Networks of Tasks), a multi-task optimization algorithm that models the task space as a graph: tasks are nodes, and edges connect tasks in the task parameter space. This representation enables knowledge transfer between tasks and remains tractable for high-dimensional problems while exploiting the topology of the task space. MONET combines social learning, which generates candidates from neighboring nodes via crossover, with individual learning, which refines a node’s own solution independently via mutation. We evaluate MONET on four domains (archery, arm, and cartpole with 5,000 tasks each; hexapod with 2,000 tasks) and show that it matches or exceeds the performance of existing MAP–Elites-based baselines across all four domains.

title: Solving Temporally Structured Decision Problems in Anticipatory Agent Networks
abstract: This article introduces a unified framework for modeling behavior of intelligent anticipatory decision-making agents (IAA). The proposed approach combines decision-theoretic foundations of IAA networks with deontic logic and temporal as well as epistemic models of agents reasoning about other agents’ beliefs and preferences. The core principle of solving decision problems in IAA networks is that a certain subset of agents influences decision choice of other agents by constraining or expanding available decision range to maximize the satisfaction of influencing agents preferences. To do so, agents simulate the rational behavior of others based on their anticipated preference structures. This anticipatory reasoning is represented through backward causation relations, linking predicted consequences to prior agents’ decisions. The evolution of the IAA network is driven by the decision-making process of an agent designated to coordinate the team. Decision-making is governed by interacting necessity, possibility, and permissibility conditions, extended over time and dependent on agents’ knowledge. Parallel decisions are aggregated using probabilistic rules. Finally, we demonstrate the framework through a simulation of temporally structured and parallel decisions in autonomous anticipatory service robot teams. This example illustrates how our approach can support the design of interaction principles in real-world mobile robotic systems modelled as IAA networks.

title: The Generation Gap: What Using Generations Misses
abstract: Evolutionary computation has produced many successful algorithms and tools. The main challenge in evolutionary computation lies not only in varying and selecting individuals but also in how they are represented, stored, scheduled, and retrieved over time. This paper introduces ARIEL, a framework that shifts evolutionary computation from focusing on generations to persistent, stateful individuals. We present three configurations: (1) synchronous, (2) archive-assisted, and (3) asynchronous. The experiments show that ARIEL’s population management can support different evolutionary workflows without changes to the underlying engine or operators. These workflows can all be achieved within the same infrastructure by adjusting eligibility conditions and orchestration logic.

title: Integer Natural Evolution Strategies
abstract: While contemporary Evolution Strategies handle integer optimization problems effectively, their adaptation mechanism is grounded in \(\ell _2\)-based Gaussian models, which are not native to the integer lattice. In contrast, the \(\ell _1\)-norm provides the natural measure of displacement on \(\mathbb {Z}^n\), with the double geometric distribution as its canonical mutation operator. In this work, we derive a fully \(\ell _1\)-native step-size adaptation mechanism from first principles and propose an Integer Natural Evolution Strategy. We show that the DG distribution belongs to the exponential family, and that its sufficient statistic |z| yields a natural-gradient signal for dispersion adaptation. By accumulating this signal via an evolution path, we obtain a fading-memory online estimator of the natural gradient, following Ollivier (2018). This establishes that DG-based step-size adaptation arises directly from the statistical structure of the mutation distribution, rather than as a discrete analog of continuous ES mechanisms. Empirical results on integer quadratic benchmarks show that INES learns meaningful coordinate-wise step-sizes and is competitive with integer-handling CMA-ES baselines. Its advantages are most visible in high-dimensional Ellipsoidal problems and in robust convergence at larger dimensions.

title: Mixed-Categorical Black-Box Optimization via Information-Geometric Bilevel Decomposition
abstract: Mixed categorical-continuous optimization arises in many practical domains, yet remains challenging. In the black-box setting, evolution strategy-based approaches have shown promise in extending the efficiency and robustness of the CMA-ES to mixed-variable spaces. However, these methods exhibit worsened performance when strong categorical-continuous interactions are present, as their underlying search distributions assume independence between categorical and continuous variables. To address this limitation, we propose a bilevel optimization framework that explicitly captures such interactions by optimizing over categorical variables in an outer loop, and over continuous variables conditioned on each categorical configuration in an inner loop. We formulate each level of the bilevel problem as a stochastic relaxation under information-geometric optimization. To mitigate the high computational cost inherent to bilevel optimization, we introduce a warm-starting strategy that accelerates the lower-level search by selecting the best among multiple cached configurations and updating the cache after each iteration. Experimental results on binary-continuous domain demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in interaction-handling capability while also being more computationally efficient across benchmarks encompassing both previously reported and newly proposed types of interaction.

title: Mixed Discrete-Continuous Optimization: Even Separable Problems Are Not That Simple
abstract: Mixed discrete–continuous optimization problems arise frequently in practice, yet remain algorithmically challenging. Although separable problems—where discrete and continuous components can be optimized independently—are often considered simple, we show that they can nonetheless present nontrivial challenges for algorithms. In this context, we introduce a refined notion of separability, termed ordinal separability, which generalizes additive decomposability and encompasses, for instance, products of positive functions, while avoiding limitations of a previous definition. We show that, for ordinally separable functions and comparison-based subspace optimizers, alternating optimization generates the same trajectory as independently optimizing each subspace subsequently. We demonstrate, on the contrary, that even the simplest separable mixed problems pose difficulties for integrated optimization approaches that apply simultaneous discrete and continuous variation operators. Simple benchmarking experiments show that combining bit-flip mutations with Gaussian mutations and success-based step size adaptation can suffer from premature convergence. This failure arises from indirect coupling between discrete and continuous components through selection, highlighting fundamental issues in mixed discrete–continuous problems, even in the most favorable separable setting.

title: Optimal Learning Parameter of the $$\sigma $$ SA-ES with Rescaled Mutations on the Rastrigin Function
abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) have been demonstrated to be effective in the optimization of continuous highly multimodal problems, provided that the population size \(\mu \) exceeds the default values employed in unimodal problems. Conversely, the efficacy of an ES can be enhanced by rescaled mutations, which reduce the step toward the new parental centroid by a factor \(1/\kappa \). Additionally, the adaptation speed of the mutation strength affects the success rate and efficiency of an ES under high multimodality. The objective of this paper is to analyze the relationship between these parameters and the search space dimension \(N\) for the \((\mu /\mu _I,\lambda )\)-\(\sigma \)SA-ES on the highly multimodal Rastrigin function. First, a scaling law is derived that depends on \(N\) and \(\mu \) in order to estimate the optimal \(\kappa \) required to achieve a satisfactory convergence probability. Second, the value of the learning parameter \(\tau \) is derived for given \(\kappa \) and \(N\), yielding optimal efficiency.

title: Quantitative Performance Analysis of Stopping Criteria for CMA-ES
abstract: Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) is a state-of-the-art black-box optimization algorithm. In general, CMA-ES uses a portfolio of multiple stopping criteria to automatically determine when to stop the search. This mechanism aims to avoid unnecessary consumption of the function evaluation budget during stagnation. Stopping criteria play an important role in CMA-ES, particularly when restart strategies are employed. However, the effectiveness of stopping criteria in CMA-ES remains poorly understood. To address this issue, this paper investigates how the 11 stopping criteria in CMA-ES behave on the noiseless BBOB function set. The performance of the stopping criteria is quantitatively evaluated based on the optimal stopping point in terms of the number of function evaluations in a single run of CMA-ES. Our results show that, although which stopping criterion is triggered first depends significantly on the sample size \(\lambda \) and the dimension n, tolflatfitness and tolfun are frequently the first criteria to be triggered among the portfolio of 11 stopping criteria. We also demonstrate that tolfunhist and the portfolio achieve the highest stopping accuracy in most cases. In addition, our results show that the tolfun and tolfunhist criteria are frequently triggered before CMA-ES reaches complete stagnation.

title: Towards Feature Selection in High-Dimensional Data: A Multi-task Evolution Strategy Aided with Symmetrical Uncertainty and Attention
abstract: Feature selection (FS) is an important data reduction technique for high-dimensional data, and evolutionary computation has become a promising solution for high-dimensional FS. However, in this regard, studies have rarely attempted to apply evolutionary strategies (ESs) based on probability distribution sampling to solve FS. In particular, the design of effective and efficient ESs for high-dimensional FS faces significant challenges. To this end, this paper proposes SAMTES, a novel multi-task ES algorithm tailored for high-dimensional FS. First, to address the challenge of high dimensionality, a hybrid task construction strategy based on symmetric uncertainty is designed, where multiple heterogeneous low-dimensional FS tasks are constructed and deployed in a multi-task optimization framework. Then, an Attention-based knowledge transfer mechanism is developed to capture the knowledge of different tasks online. Finally, a mathematically formulated update procedure is executed to iteratively update the probability distribution of each task based on adaptive weighting of the knowledge of distinct tasks. By integrating these key components, SAMTES offers a novel scalable framework for efficiently applying ESs to high-dimensional data. Comprehensive experiments on a series of real-world datasets (whose dimensions range from 2,000 to 100,000) demonstrate that when tackling high-dimensional FS problems, SAMTES achieves superior classification results within less running time, overall outperforming other state-of-the-art peers in terms of both performance and efficiency.

title: Adaptive Protection for Evolutionary Feature Construction in Symbolic Regression with Application to Credit Classification
abstract: Evolutionary feature construction has shown strong promise in symbolic regression by automatically discovering informative transformations of input features that enhance a simple base learner. However, existing approaches often lack explicit mechanisms to preserve important constructed features discovered during evolution, and valuable genetic material can be lost when genetic operators disrupt effective features. This paper introduces an adaptive protection mechanism that leverages feature importance metrics to selectively preserve constructed features during evolution. The mechanism provides stronger protection for more important constructed features while still allowing less important features to be modified and to incorporate useful building blocks from more important features. We evaluate the approach using multiple feature importance calculation methods and demonstrate its robustness across different base learners. Experimental results on 98 regression benchmark datasets show that the proposed mechanism consistently improves solution quality over baseline approaches, and experiments on two credit classification datasets demonstrate that the method also extends effectively to improve search effectiveness beyond symbolic regression.

title: Multi-modal Learning Meets Genetic Programming: Analyzing Alignment in Latent Space Optimization
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) aims to discover mathematical expressions from data, a task traditionally tackled using Genetic Programming (GP) through combinatorial search over symbolic structures. Latent Space Optimization (LSO) methods use neural encoders to map symbolic expressions into continuous spaces, transforming the combinatorial search into continuous optimization. SNIP (Meidani et al., 2024), a contrastive pre-training model inspired by CLIP, advances LSO by introducing a multi-modal approach: aligning symbolic and numeric encoders in a shared latent space to learn the phenotype-genotype mapping, enabling optimization in the numeric space to implicitly guide symbolic search. However, this relies on fine-grained cross-modal alignment, whereas literature on similar models like CLIP reveals that such an alignment is typically coarse-grained. In this paper, we investigate whether SNIP delivers on its promise of effective bi-modal optimization for SR. Our experiments show that: (1) cross-modal alignment does not improve during optimization, even as fitness increases, and (2) the alignment learned by SNIP is too coarse to efficiently conduct principled search in the symbolic space. These findings reveal that while multi-modal LSO holds significant potential for SR, effective alignment-guided optimization remains unrealized in practice, highlighting fine-grained alignment as a critical direction for future work.

title: Order-Aware GSGP in Active Factor Allocation
abstract: A recent extension of geometric semantic genetic programming (GSGP) is order-aware GSGP. This approach employs geometric semantic operators for real-valued functions to directly search for functions that match the target output ordering behaviour using the Kemeny distance metric, while maintaining a unimodal fitness landscape. Factor timing is an active investment strategy that adjusts portfolio exposure to risk factors expected to outperform. Since the task is fundamentally about ranking factors, order-aware GSGP is a natural fit. We evaluate the efficacy of order-aware GSGP in this context. Our empirical results show that order-aware GSGP significantly outperforms standard GP with Kemeny distance as a fitness function, suggesting a critical role for the unimodality of the fitness landscape in order semantic space. Portfolios constructed using order-aware GSGP achieve higher mean returns and lower turnover than those built with traditional GSGP. Strategies derived from order-aware GSGP also outperform a static equal-weight benchmark that most active investment approaches fail to beat, even after accounting for transaction costs.

title: Prior Coverage and Search Bias in Multiview Symbolic Regression
abstract: Structural prior initialization, which seeds part of the population with templates such as polynomials, trigonometric terms, and rational expressions, dramatically improves symbolic regression (SR), but the dependence on prior quality remains uncharacterized. We study this in multiview SR, which jointly fits several related datasets by decomposing each prediction into a shared core equation and view-specific residuals. We introduce a prior coverage framework characterizing an initialization library along two axes: coverage (the fraction of the target’s structural components the library can represent) and diversity (the breadth of templates beyond target-matching ones). In a factorial study of 3 equation families \(\times \) 7 prior regimes \(\times \) 30 seeds (3,780 runs), we find three behavioral regimes. When the target is reachable (assemblable within the search budget), higher coverage yields lower median loss (Spearman \(\rho = -0.917\), \(p = 0.004\)), and diversity adds further gains at equal coverage (\(p < 0.001\)). When the two trade off, a broad generic library at coverage 0.67 outperforms a narrow matched library at coverage 1.0. On unreachable targets all priors fail and complex templates trap search in local optima. A search-dynamics analysis (450 runs) reveals the mechanisms: seeded-lineage survival does not predict performance, structural diversity collapses by generation 15, and seeded subexpressions (motifs) largely vanish by generation 20: initialization helps by routing search into productive regions, not by preserving seeded structures. Prior effectiveness thus hinges on the interaction of coverage, diversity, and reachability.

title: SemanticViz: Analyzing Semantic Space Exploration of Ensemble Methods
abstract: Ensembles of decision trees and Geometric Semantic Genetic Programming (GSGP) both build accurate regressors by aggregating weak learners, yet their exploration of the model’s output semantic space differs in ways that performance metrics cannot reveal. We pair interactive 2D and 3D dimensionality-reduction visualizations with a quantitative metric framework spanning two families: trajectory metrics (path length, straightness, target alignment, step-size schedule, effective dimensionality) and coverage metrics (cloud spread, centroid-to-target, total variance), and use it to compare six ensemble methods across five tabular regression benchmarks. We compare kPCA-cosine, t-SNE, and UMAP qualitatively and via trustworthiness and continuity scores, adopting kPCA-cosine for the visualizations; distance-sensitive metrics are computed in the original semantic space.Three contrasts emerge.Batch Random Forest and Extra Trees weak learners cluster tightly near the target; boosting weak learners (XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting) cluster tightly far from it; the GSGP population spans an order-of-magnitude wider neighborhood than either.GSGP learning trajectories are roughly \(3\times \) longer than boosting’s, in essentially uncorrelated steps perpendicular to the toward-target direction, and this regime holds population-wide rather than only for the eventual elite.These contrasts identify GSGP-style exploration paired with boosted-tree exploitation as a promising hybrid direction.

title: Strongly-Typed Geometric Syntactic Genetic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces Strongly-Typed Geometric Syntactic Genetic Programming (ST-GSynGP), an extension of Geometric Syntactic Genetic Programming (GSynGP), which is a tree-based Geometric GP variant that leverages geometric crossover in syntactic space to implicitly mitigate bloat and preserve locality. ST-GSynGP improves GSynGP’s applicability for complex problems by accommodating strongly typed and variable-arity functions directly into the geometric crossover mechanism. ST-GSynGP is compared to Strongly-typed Genetic Programming (STGP) across symbolic regression, Boolean logic, classification, and control benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that ST-GSynGP achieves competitive performance while consistently producing more compact and interpretable solutions. These findings demonstrate that combining strong typing with geometric syntactic recombination provides an effective foundation for evolving high-performing and interpretable machine learning models for a wide range of applications.

title: Structure vs. Constants: A Study of Coefficients in Cartesian Genetic Programming
abstract: Cartesian genetic programming (CGP) represents programs as directed acyclic graphs, making it well suited for evolving functional expressions with multiple inputs and outputs. A key yet often overlooked aspect of cartesian genetic programming (CGP) is the role of numerical coefficients, which can significantly influence both the expressiveness and efficiency of evolved solutions. Such coefficients are important not only for improving performance, but also for preventing unnecessary over-complexification of graph structures. In this work, we conduct an extensive study of the role of coefficients in CGP. We investigate multiplicative and additive coefficients applied to nodes or connections and we consider two optimization strategies: Gaussian mutation embedded within the standard CGP mutation process, and gradient-based optimization using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) within a nested optimization loop. To systematically evaluate these design choices, we employ symbolic regression (SR) as a controlled and computationally efficient benchmark. Our results on nine real-world SR datasets show an overall positive impact of coefficients on accuracy, with multiplicative coefficients being more influential than additive ones, and gradient-based optimization consistently outperforming Gaussian mutation. Moreover, we observe that coefficient optimization can often be deferred to a post-processing step with little or no loss in performance.

title: Symbolic Regression for Shared Expressions – Introducing Partial Parameter Sharing
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to find symbolic expressions that describe datasets. Due to its inherent interpretability, Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful paradigm for scientific discovery. Recent advances have expanded SR to describe related phenomena using a single expression with varying sets of parameters, thereby introducing a single categorical variable. To illustrate, this enables the search for a single expression describing temperature-dependent viscosity across multiple fluids, while simultaneously identifying a distinct set of fluid-specific parameters. We expand upon prior efforts by considering multiple categorical variables and introducing intermediate levels of parameter sharing. Rather than parameters being either entirely universal or entirely unique, some parameters can also be shared across specific categories while remaining distinct for others. This allows for separating universal effects (shared parameters), category-specific trends (partially-shared parameters), and category interactions (non-shared parameters). We test the limits of this setup in terms of reducing data requirements and transfer learning using a synthetic, fitting-only example. Furthermore, we apply the method to an astrophysics dataset also used in a previous single-category study. In comparison, we achieve similar fit quality with significantly fewer parameters while extracting additional information about the problem.

title: Towards ML-Based Position-Aware Mutation Operator in Cartesian Genetic Programming
abstract: Cartesian Genetic Programming (CGP) relies primarily on point mutation, which is uninformed and treats all genes uniformly. Combined with positional bias – nodes near inputs being substantially more likely to be active – most mutations target irrelevant parts of the chromosome. Existing approaches address this by restructuring the genotype; in this paper, the mutation operator itself is made position-aware. The Mean number of Active Output Connections (MAOC), a theoretical metric quantifying positional bias from CGP parameters alone, is derived and validated against an archive of over 11 million mutation records from CGP runs on the PMLB dataset. Three operators of increasing complexity are proposed: probability-based, Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based, and Large Language Model (LLM)-based. Evaluation on 38 symbolic regression tasks shows all three achieve fitness comparable to baseline while accelerating convergence in the early generations of evolutionary search. The probability-based operator reduces runtime by approximately 32 % compared to baseline point mutation, while the GNN-based operator adds runtime overhead of approximately only 21 %.

title: Enhancing Quality-Diversity with Adaptive Heterogeneous Operator Allocation
abstract: Quality-Diversity (QD) optimization is a paradigm that seeks to discover a large collection of solutions that are both high-performing and behaviorally diverse. While the representative PGA-MAP-Elites algorithm enhances exploration by integrating Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Policy Gradient (PG) operators, it encounters several critical bottlenecks: the constrained exploration range of GA mutation, the dilution of high-value samples during PG training, and computational inefficiencies resulting from rigid operator allocation ratios. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Ada-HOME, an Adaptive Heterogeneous Operator-allocated MAP-Elites algorithm. At the bottom level of the algorithm, the search operators are reconstructed: a discrete gene crossover mechanism is introduced into the GA operator to facilitate the leapfrog recombination of elite individuals, thereby boosting divergent exploration; meanwhile, a dual experience replay buffer is incorporated into the PG operator to prevent the rapid loss of high-quality exploration data and accelerate directional convergence. At the top level of the algorithm, the high-level operator scheduling process is modeled as a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) decision problem, enabling the adaptive adjustment of allocation ratios through a reward mechanism based on successful sample generation. Experimental results across six standard benchmarks demonstrate that Ada-HOME overcomes the efficiency bottlenecks of the baseline algorithm with static allocation, exhibiting superior optimization performance.

title: Generation of Diverse and Functional Robot Designs Using Superquadrics Parametrisation and Quality-Diversity
abstract: Generative design of robots requires navigating a vast search-space, encompassing physical configurations and behavioural parameters. Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) have shown promising results, but often converge prematurely to a small set of sub-optimal designs. To counter premature convergence, we introduce a superquadrics-based representation (SQs) for robot bodies. SQs are interpretable, compact and computationally efficient mathematical representations of 3D geometrical shapes that can be tuned to specific design-spaces. To encourage morphological diversity, we combine this representation with a quality-diversity (QD) algorithm (MAP-Elites). We compare SQs and Compositional Pattern Producing Networks representations as generators of morphologies, combining them with standard EAs and MAP-Elites. In two test environments, we find that using SQs to generate morphology in conjunction with the MAP-Elites algorithm reaches the highest QD-score across both environments, maximising diversity of design and functionality of generated robots. The findings highlight the benefits of using a compact and interpretable geometric representation for exploring a complex design-space and suggest that combining SQs with an explicit diversity mechanism increases the quality and number of designs generated.

title: BNTGP: A Hyper-Heuristic Balancing Non-Dominated Tournament Genetic Programming for Multi-Objective Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem
abstract: This paper presents a generative genetic programming hyper-heuristic (GPHH) Balancing Non-dominated Tournament Genetic Programming (BNTGP) for the multi-objective (MO) multi-skill resource constrained project scheduling problem (MS-RCPSP). The proposed approach differs from the existing state-of-the-art metaheuristics for MS-RCPSP by evolving a set of GP trees. Each tree guides the selection of a feasible task-resource pair during scheduling, based on task and resource features. The method uses a wide range of problem characteristics for the MS-RCPSP, including 16 newly proposed ones, making it suitable for the considered problem. The proposed approach is inspired by the Balanced Non-dominated Tournament Genetic Algorithm (BNTGA), utilizing the archive of non-dominated individuals as the main selection pool, and gap selection favors sparsely populated regions of the archive. The BNTGP was tested on six benchmark MO MS-RCPSP instances, and its performance was compared with state-of-the-art metaheuristics, namely MOEA/D, NSGA-II, NTGA2, and BNTGA. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach using standard MO quality measures, demonstrating the method’s potential to automate the construction of pairwise GP trees for MS-RCPSP.

title: Novelty-Based Generation of Continuous Landscapes with Diverse Local Optima Networks
abstract: Local Optima Networks (LONs) encode the global structure of search spaces as graphs, but their construction requires iterative execution of a search algorithm to identify local optima and approximate the transitions between Basins of Attraction (BoAs). In continuous optimization, the high cost of search-based LON construction precludes the assembly of instance sets that systematically cover the LON feature space, leaving the LON feature–performance link largely unexamined. To address this, we propose a search-free LON construction for Max-Set of Gaussians (MSG) landscapes, a problem class with explicitly tunable multimodality. Our alternative BoA definition bypasses search-based BoA identification, enabling low-cost LON construction. We further leverage Novelty Search (NS) to explore the parameter space of MSG landscapes, generating instances with diverse graph topologies. Our experiments show that the alternative BoAs closely align with gradient-based BoAs, and that NS successfully generates MSG landscapes with varied search difficulty and connectivity patterns among optima. Finally, on the instances generated by our methods, LON features accurately predict the success rates of two well-established evolutionary algorithms.

title: Quality Diversity for Reliable Data Driven Time-Use Optimization
abstract: The daily allocation of the finite 24-h time budget is strongly associated with physical, mental, and cognitive health. While predictive models can estimate the relationship between time-use compositions and health outcomes such as body mass index, life satisfaction, and cognition, most optimization approaches focus only on maximizing expected benefit and do not consider the uncertainty inherent in data-driven prediction. Ignoring uncertainty in health-related decisions can lead to unrealistic time-use recommendations. To address this gap, we introduce an uncertainty quantification Quality Diversity (QD) framework for a more reliable time-use recommendation. Objective functions are derived using compositional data analysis using a large child cohort dataset \(n > 1000\), to capture the relationship between daily activity compositions and multiple health indicators. We develop a new approach that incorporates predictive uncertainty into QD processes and produces more reliable recommendations that balance the expected health benefits with the confidence of the model. We explore the solution space through variable-based and objective-based behavioral representations, revealing diverse high-quality time-use composition and explicit relationships between health outcomes under uncertainty. By embedding uncertainty directly into optimization, our framework shifts the time-use recommendations toward regions of lower uncertainty while preserving high-quality structures for more reliable decision-making in behavioral health.

title: U-Net-Accelerated Quality-Diversity Optimization for Climate-Adaptive Urban Layouts
abstract: Optimizing urban layouts for climate adaptation requires balancing building density with cold-air ventilation. Because physics-based climate simulations are computationally expensive, planners typically evaluate fewer than ten manual designs. Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms offer a way to systematically illuminate the design space, but they require surrogate models to be practical.In this paper, we replace a slow, regulatory physics simulator with a spatial deep-learning surrogate (U-Net) inside an offline MAP-Elites loop. We systematically compare this spatial approach with a traditional Gaussian Process (GP) surrogate across different training-data strategies (quasi-random Sobol sampling vs. active QD bootstrapping). Our results reveal that scalar GP surrogates fail catastrophically when trained on random samples, requiring expensive, actively generated QD archives to generalize. In contrast, the spatial inductive bias of the U-Net allows it to learn the underlying physics mapping robustly (\(R^2 = 0.996\)), completely independent of the training data source. This allows offline QD optimization to achieve highly accurate fitness rankings (\(\rho = 0.994\)) using only a one-time batch of random training samples. The resulting pipeline, deployed in the open-source OpenSKIZZE tool, generates thousands of diverse, climate-evaluated building layouts in under ten minutes.

title: A New Encoding to Mitigate Representation Biases in Morphological Robot Evolution
abstract: Modular robot morphologies in evolutionary robotics are frequently represented using Compositional Pattern Producing Networks (CPPNs) decoded via breadth-first search (BFS). We identify and analyse a previously overlooked representational bias of this approach causing evolved populations converge to hinge-dominated body plans. We also show that CPPN-based encodings exhibit rotation non-invariance, substantial memory overhead, and genotypes that are resistant to compression. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel representation, Neural Developmental Encoding (NDE) with highest-probability decoding (HPD), where morphologies are derived from connection probability matrices produced by a fixed decoder network operating on compact embedding vectors. Our experiments reveal that NDE+HPD significantly outperforms CPPN+BFS, achieving a 40% increase in fitness and a 32% boost in population diversity, while reducing the average hinge-to-module ratio from 0.99 to 0.68. Thus, this study resolves a previously unnoticed bias in CPPNs and provides quantitative evidence that the choice of genetic encoding is a crucial design decision, as it profoundly shapes the set of morphologies that evolution can search and discover.

title: GSAM: A Generalizable and Safe Robotic Framework for Articulated Object Manipulation
abstract: Articulated object manipulation is a unique challenge for service robots. Existing methods employ end-to-end policy learning, vision-motion planning, and large-language/visual-language model (LLM/VLM), but often overlook the diversity of articulated objects and the complexity of interactions between end-effector and handle, leading to limited generalization and destructive collisions. To address this, we propose GSAM, a generalizable and safe robotic framework for articulated object manipulation. Specifically, a vision-based perceiver generates the kinematic parameters. Considering that pre-trained markers in perceiver yield raw estimations that may deviate from commonsense, we present a fine-tuned VLM-based refiner, using chain-of-thought (COT) commonsense reasoning to refine perception. To prevent destructive collisions, we design an interaction constraint function generator, integrating articulated object, interaction pose, and obstacle avoidance knowledge into a base. LLM then functionalize these constraints and apply them to trajectory and posture planning. A kinematic-aware manipulation planner verifies reachability for trajectory and posture. Experiments on 50 hinge tasks across 5 object categories and 50 randomly initialized end-effector-handle configurations show that GSAM reduces standard deviation by 3.1% and improves manipulation success rate by 36.0% compared to the best baseline, respectively demonstrating the superior object generalization and interaction safety of GSAM in practical scenarios.

title: Lens-Descriptor Guided Evolutionary Algorithm for Optimization of Complex Optical Systems with Glass Choice
abstract: Fixed-structure lens design is a high-dimensional mixed integer problem with many local minima: radii and distances are continuous, glass choices are discrete, and in practice, designers need a portfolio of strong alternatives rather than a single optimum. We address this challenge with the novel Lens-Descriptor Guided Evolutionary Algorithm (LDG-EA), a parallel multimodal optimization method for fixed-structure optical design with explicit glass choice. LDG-EA turns an optics notion of structural similarity into a search primitive: it partitions the design space into interpretable descriptor classes defined by radius-sign patterns and glass identities, learns which classes are promising, and runs descriptor-constrained searches in parallel. This makes diversity explicit, allocation of computational resources efficient, and the search naturally scalable on modern parallel hardware. On the six-element Double-Gauss benchmark, LDG-EA outperforms the considered quality-diversity, multimodal, and lens-specific baselines in runtime, diversity, and solution quality under the same computational budget . Across five runs, it identifies more than 400 high-quality local-minimum candidates on average and, in total over five runs, finds 403 designs that outperform the locally optimized Double-Gauss reference lens. These results position LDG-EA as a practical route to time-to-portfolio optimization in optics for the Double-Gauss structure and as a promising template for search in other structured engineering design problems.

title: Morphological Evolution of Aerial Robots: Comparing Genetic Encodings
abstract: Evolutionary robotics has long debated direct versus generative encodings, but most evidence comes from terrestrial and aquatic robots, where imperfect morphologies still yield functional (albeit poor) behaviour and thus useful fitness signal. Aerial robots differ in that the boundary between functional and nonfunctional designs is sharp, and small morphological changes can produce configurations incapable of hovering. This motivates our study on encodings in a domain where the border between viable and non-viable designs is sharp. We evolve hexacopter morphologies using direct, indirect, and hybrid encodings, combined with a geometric controller individually tuned to each morphology, and compare them under standard and speciation-based evolution. Without speciation, CPPN-based methods outperform direct encoding. With speciation, this trend reverses. We attribute the CPPN drop to low-locality mutations producing scattered offspring that speciation fails to refine. Overall, the hybrid encoding is the most robust across settings.

title: Pattern Layout Optimization for Seam-Aware Texture Alignment
abstract: When assembling a garment from patterned fabric, periodic motifs such as stripes or checks should continue seamlessly across seam lines, yet the two subproblems involved, nesting (minimising fabric waste) and texture alignment (matching pattern phase at seams), are mostly studied in isolation. Prior texture-alignment work assumes an unbounded fabric supply and deforms 2D patch shapes directly, leaving garment fit changes implicit and unmeasured. We propose the first joint optimisation of fabric efficiency, seam-wise texture alignment, and fit preservation. Our key idea is to optimise seam positions on the 3D body mesh rather than deforming flat patterns: this grounds every modification in body geometry, making fit deviation an explicit, measurable objective. Texture periodicity is modelled via wallpaper symmetry groups, covering eight pattern families including herringbone, chevron, and brick bond. We solve the resulting mixed search space (continuous seam parameters, discrete phase offsets, grain orientations) with a mixed-integer evolution strategy using variable-specific operators. Experiments on three garment types with up to 2,200 pattern pieces show consistent improvement in texture alignment over all baselines including random search at matched evaluation budget.

title: A Fresh Look at Lamarckian Evolution and the Baldwin Effect
abstract: Baldwinian and Lamarckian evolution have existed for a long time in evolutionary algorithms (EAs) without ever dominating the academic literature or practical applications. In this work, we use modern empirical and theoretical methods to revisit Lamarckian and Baldwinian evolution and rigorously compare them with the generic Darwinian evolution. On the empirical side, we run a comprehensive suite of experiments on graphs from six different datasets from the recent GraphBench benchmark on Maximum Independent Set and Maximum Cut problems. Our results show that Baldwinian and Lamarckian evolution consistently outperform Darwinian evolution, confirming the great potential of local search augmented evolutionary algorithms. Notably, in the great majority of cases, all EAs outperform recent deep learning baselines and approach the performance of highly specialised heuristic and exact solvers. We furthermore report a high-performing set of generalist parameters for all studied evolution types that we hope will be of use to practitioners in future. On the theoretical side, we extend the existing DeceptiveLeadingBlocks benchmark to arbitrary block length k. For all constant k, we then prove asymptotically tight runtime bounds for the \((1+1)\) EA in the three evolution types on this benchmark. For Baldwinian evolution, these are independent of k, whereas for the other two evolution types, the runtimes steeply increase with growing value of k.

title: Coevolutionary Federated Learning with Differential Privacy
abstract: Decentralized federated learning eliminates the central-server bottleneck of standard federated learning, but shared model updates can still leak sensitive information through membership inference attacks. We propose Coevolutionary Federated Learning with Differential Privacy (CoEvo-DP), a decentralized framework that combines cooperative coevolution of autoencoder components with peer-to-peer parameter exchange and differentially private local optimization. Each client communicates only with its immediate neighbors, removing the central server as both a bottleneck and a single point of failure while bounding data leakage through formal \((\varepsilon , \delta )\)-DP guarantees. On MedMNIST medical image benchmarks across MLP and CNN architectures, CoEvo-DP improves reconstruction quality over centralized differentially private federated learning under matched privacy budgets, with the strongest gains on CNN models and high-resolution inputs, while maintaining comparable resistance to reconstruction-based membership inference attacks.

title: Efficient Imitation-Based Rule Learning for Online Yard Crane Scheduling via Order-Aware Geometric Semantic Genetic Programming
abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) for evolving scheduling rules often relies on expensive simulation-based evaluations, which provide limited guidance and may lead to slow convergence. Existing research mitigates expensive simulation through instance subsampling or surrogate evaluation, but subsampling often yields noisy and unstable fitness signals, whereas surrogate models heavily rely on previously seen samples for accurate prediction. In this work, imitating near-optimal decision-point-wise behaviour to explicitly guide scheduling rule learning to speed up convergence is explored. Since such target behaviour is not readily available, a method is proposed to derive near-optimal target behaviour on representative decision points. As scheduling rules select actions by comparing rule-generated scores, making relative orderings more important than absolute output values, the derived target behaviour is naturally expressed via action orderings. This makes Order-aware Geometric Semantic GP (O-GSGP) a natural fit for searching effectively in this ordering-behaviour semantic space. In addition, since interpretability is important in scheduling rule learning, an ordering-behaviour-preserving pruning mechanism is introduced to control rule growth induced by geometric semantic operators. Experiments on the online Yard Crane scheduling problem show that the resulting scheduling-adapted O-GSGP achieves better average performance than standard GP and several advanced acceleration methods when the guiding target semantics are computationally cheap, behaviourally general, and strong.

title: Exploring Competitive Coevolution for N-Player Synthetic Game Trees
abstract: In order to enable better analysis of competitive coevolutionary algorithms (CoEAs) across a wide variety of problems, particularly games with different numbers of players, we test them against specialized synthetic game trees representing procedurally-generated novel games with up to ten players. We introduce an algorithm to parameterize these game trees by several properties, including the payoff structure, player count, and the rate of transpositions in the tree. By testing across thousands of synthetic game trees, we are able to investigate the sensitivity of CoEA performance to different game-theoretic properties. We demonstrate the applications of this technique by using it to measure the impact of several coevolutionary parameters, including the introduction of a hall of fame. We present results showing that CoEA performance can be very sensitive to the payoff structure of games in particular.

title: Evolving Features vs Evolving Entire Trees with GP for Interpretable Survival Analysis
abstract: Survival analysis concerns the task of predicting the time until an event occurs. Often used in the medical field, survival analysis deals with incomplete (i.e., censored) data, for instance, from patients who did not experience the event during the duration of the study. For practical use, both accuracy and interpretability are important. Survival trees are easy-to-follow survival models that split the patient cohort recursively into discrete patient groups. Whilst survival trees can capture complex relationships in survival problems, to do so accurately, they typically need to grow large, threatening interpretability. Moreover, survival trees are often built using greedy approaches that may overlook globally optimal split combinations, limiting predictive performance. Shallow survival trees require expressive, higher-order feature combinations to achieve competitive accuracy. We therefore use genetic programming to multi-objectively evolve inherently inspectable feature sets and study how they interact with different tree induction strategies. We further introduce an evolutionary approach that jointly optimises the survival tree structure and the non-linear split logic. Our findings demonstrate that evolutionary feature construction improves predictive performance across different tree induction strategies on two real-world datasets and two different survival tree depths. Given its speed and flexible presentation, the multi-objective evolution of entire trees holds the most future promise.

title: GeneABAC: ABAC Policy Generation Optimized by Genetic Programming
abstract: For many players in the computer industry, the current state of access control is built on role-based access control (RBAC), where the criteria for granting access are based on group membership, resulting in policies that become difficult to manage and optimize manually. This management challenge leads to significant overpermissioning. To address this, we introduce GeneABAC, a novel genetic programming framework that evolves attribute-based access control (ABAC) policies from access logs. GeneABAC employs a hierarchical island-based model integrated with bootstrap aggregating to evolve Boolean policy trees through multiple isolated populations. These populations utilize a bidirectional co-evolution mechanism to exchange genetic material, achieving improved generalization while maintaining strict rule compactness. Empirical evaluations show that the proposed hierarchical approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving substantial F1 score improvements on three out of four benchmark datasets. GeneABAC improves security by producing concise, interpretable, and generalizable policies that balance performance with maintainability and avoid blocking legitimate user activity.

title: GPAS: Multi-objective Genetic Programming with AUC and Separability Measures for Multiclass Classification
abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) exhibits strong performance on binary classification tasks, yet its effectiveness diminishes when applied to multiclass problems. A prevalent approach in GP for multiclass classification involves decomposing a K-class problem into K binary subproblems using the one-versus-rest (OVR) strategy. However, this decomposition tends to introduce two challenges: class imbalance and the resulting classifiers often rely on predefined thresholds for label prediction. Being a threshold-independent evaluation metric, the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) has been widely adopted as a fitness function in GP to tackle class imbalance. Nevertheless, AUC-optimized classifiers still require a predefined threshold to determine the class labels of test instances. In this paper, we propose a threshold-free multi-objective GP approach (GPAS) for multiclass classification. To handle data imbalance, the first objective employs an AUC approximation to improve the overall ranking performance of binary classifiers under imbalanced settings. To further overcome the threshold limitation of AUC-optimized classifiers, the second objective introduces a separability measure to maximize the divergence among different classes. Building upon this, a threshold-free reference-based label prediction strategy is proposed to assign final class labels to test instances. Experimental results on eight multiclass datasets demonstrate that, compared with other GP-based methods, our proposed method achieves comparable or significantly better results.

title: GP-GOMEA with GPU-Based Fitness Evaluations: Design and Performance Analysis
abstract: GP-GOMEA is a state-of-the-art evolutionary algorithm for symbolic regression, known for discovering small and interpretable models. However, its computational cost remains substantial, limiting its applicability to larger datasets and more complex target expressions. In contrast, the rise of modern subsymbolic approaches, particularly deep learning, has been driven largely by the massive parallelism offered by GPUs. In this work, we take the first major step toward a fully GPU-accelerated GP-GOMEA by introducing a GPU-based fitness evaluation scheme. We design a GPU-friendly representation of GP-GOMEA’s template-based individuals and a corresponding evaluation strategy that exploits the inherent parallelism of population-based search. This substantially increases evaluation throughput, enabling orders of magnitude more evaluations within the same time budget. Across four standard symbolic regression benchmarks, this increased evaluation capacity yields performance improvements, particularly for larger datasets and larger population sizes. Moreover, the ability to efficiently evaluate much larger datasets and more complex templates enables analyses that were previously infeasible, allowing us to systematically analyze what makes expressions increasingly difficult for GP-GOMEA, providing new insights into how expression structure affects search difficulty. Finally, for the first time, this expanded capability allows a problem-agnostic evolutionary algorithm to reliably regress one of the largest Feynman equations within four hours.

title: Inferring Structural Causal Models from Data with Grammatical Evolution
abstract: Causal models allow representing complex systems by going beyond statistical correlations and explicitly capturing cause–effect relationships among variables. Structural causal models (SCMs) offer a rigorous formalism to describe causal models, encoding, in the form of equations systems, both the causal graph that specifies directional dependencies among variables and the functional mechanisms governing these relationships. Among SCMs, additive noise models (ANMs) include exogenous stochasticity, hence capturing noisy data. In practice, the underlying causal structure is rarely known a priori and must be inferred from data. This is a challenging task, as it requires jointly identifying the causal graph and the associated structural equations. We propose an evolutionary approach for learning SCMs from data. We express ANMs as probabilistic programs and use grammatical evolution for synthesizing them. Our contribution comprises a dedicated grammar, formally yielding ANMs, and a fitness function that accounts for (a) statistical adequacy of the candidate ANM with respect to the observed data, quantified via the likelihood, and quality of the causal structure, assessed by computing likelihoods under the candidate ANM when interventions are applied. (b) We assess experimentally our approach on five problems and show that it infers effective and simple causal models from data.

title: Informative Decision Situation Selection for Phenotypic Characterization-Based Surrogate-Assisted Genetic Programming in Dynamic Container Terminal Truck Scheduling
abstract: Surrogate-assisted genetic programming (SAGP) addresses the computational challenge of evolving heuristics for dynamic scheduling by replacing expensive fitness evaluations with learned approximations. However, standard surrogate models require fixed-size inputs, whereas GP individuals are variable-sized symbolic programs, making characterization a core challenge. Phenotypic characterization (PC) observes each individual’s behavior over a selected set of decision situations (DSs), where each DS captures a scheduling decision moment and its candidate actions. The selected DSs therefore determine what behavioral evidence is available to the surrogate model. Existing studies typically use fixed DS sets that are randomly sampled or left unspecified, leaving the construction of informative DS sets under a fixed observation budget as an open question. In this paper, we study informative DS selection for PC-based SAGP in dynamic container terminal truck scheduling (DCTTS). We develop a multi-stage framework that first collects a broad raw DS pool using committee policies and constructs a representative candidate pool, then applies Alignment-Guided Quality-Coverage Greedy (AQCG) to select complementary DSs within this observation budget. AQCG measures DS informativeness by quantifying how well each DS’s induced behavioral distinctions align with true performance differences, then greedily maximizes set-level coverage of this alignment information. Experimental results on DCTTS show that AQCG achieves the best overall scheduling performance among the compared methods and improves surrogate guidance over random sampling and quality-only selection.
